0.title: Nehemiah: The God Who Remembers
0.overview:
The book of Nehemiah opens with a question. A Jewish official in the Persian palace at Susa, the king's cupbearer, asks travellers from Judah how things are in Jerusalem, and hears that the survivors are in great trouble and shame (1:3) and the wall is broken down. He weeps, and prays for four months before he says a word to the king. The book that records a wall built in fifty-two days begins with a man on his knees.

In the Hebrew Bible Ezra and Nehemiah are one book. Nehemiah arrives in 445 BC, thirteen years after Ezra, and the story falls into three parts. Chapters 1-7: the wall, built against mockery, threats, a debt crisis and plots, and finished with the help of our God (6:16). Chapters 8-10: the law read and explained, the people told that the joy of the LORD is your strength (8:10), a great prayer of confession, and a covenant sealed. Chapters 11-13: the city peopled, the wall dedicated with joy, and then Nehemiah returns from the Persian court to find almost every promise of the covenant broken.

Much of the book is Nehemiah's own memoir, and he is one of the most vivid men in the Bible: afraid before the king and going in anyway, praying in the pause between a question and an answer (2:4), refusing his governor's allowance for twelve years, throwing an enemy's furniture out of a temple chamber. And all through it he prays one prayer: remember. He begins by asking God to remember the word he gave Moses (1:8), and his last words are Remember me, O my God, for good (13:31).

The book is honest. It lets a register stand whose figures do not add up to its own total, reports that the high priest's grandson married Sanballat's daughter (13:28), and ends not in triumph but with a governor putting the same reforms in place a second time. Several of the lists are treated here by what they mean rather than name by name; the prayers of chapters 1 and 9 and the reading of chapter 8 are treated at length.

And the book points beyond itself. Nehemiah confesses his people's sins as we, and one Intercessor took on sins that were not his (2 Cor 5:21). His enemies accused him of letting prophets proclaim a king in Judah (6:7); it was false of him and true of the King Zechariah had promised (Zech 9:9), who died under the charge the King of the Jews. The joy of the Feast of Booths waited for the day when Jesus cried out, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). The covenant the people signed could not change a heart, and the book leaves us waiting for the one that does: I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33).

Its closing chapter is the latest history the Old Testament tells, and its last word is a prayer. Four and a half centuries later, outside the walls of the same city, a dying man prayed almost the same words, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom, and was answered at once: today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:42-43). The God of Nehemiah is the God who remembers.

1.title: The Man Who Wept for a City
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now it happened in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel,<sup>2</sup>that Hanani, one of my brothers, came with certain men from Judah. And I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And they said to me, "The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire."<sup>4</sup>As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.<sup>5</sup>And I said, "O LORD God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,<sup>6</sup>let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned.<sup>7</sup>We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses.<sup>8</sup>Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, 'If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples,<sup>9</sup>but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.'<sup>10</sup>They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.<sup>11</sup>O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man." Now I was cupbearer to the king.
1.overview: In Chislev of Artaxerxes' twentieth year (about 445 BC), Nehemiah, a Jew serving in the Persian palace at Susa, hears that the survivors in Judah are in great trouble and shame and the wall is broken down (vv. 1-3), perhaps the old ruin of 586 BC, perhaps the fresh wreck of the attempt Artaxerxes himself had stopped (Ezra 4:21-23). He weeps, fasts and prays for four months (v. 4; cf. 2:1). The prayer (vv. 5-11) is built almost entirely from Scripture: Daniel's address to God, Solomon's plea to be heard, a confession that includes his own house, Moses' warning and promise, and Moses' argument after the golden calf. Only at the end are we told who is praying: the king's cupbearer.
1.theology:
Nehemiah prays God's own words back to him. The threat of scattering had been kept to the letter; therefore the promise of gathering will be kept too. That is the ground of all confident prayer: not the strength of our feeling, but the fact that God has spoken and does not go back on his word.

He confesses as we and pleads that the people are God's by redemption. Both movements point beyond him. The true Intercessor took on sins that were not his (2 Cor 5:21), pleads for a people bought with his own blood (1 Pet 1:18-19), and stands not as a trembling cupbearer before a Persian king but at the right hand of the Father, where he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25).
1.examples:
Nehemiah's first act in his own book is to ask how God's people are.

Susa the citadel is Esther's address; God had put his people in that palace before.

He prayed for four months before he said a word to the king.

He was born in exile, and he still said I and my father's house have sinned.

The king he prayed about had signed the order stopping the wall, until a decree is made by me.

We learn he is the king's cupbearer only after he has finished praying.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Wall of Jerusalem Is Broken Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Susa, Nehemiah asks his brother Hanani about Jerusalem and its survivors (vv. 1-3). The news is bad on both counts, and he weeps, fasts and prays before the God of heaven (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The book that will record a wall built in fifty-two days opens with a man who does nothing for four months but pray. That order is not incidental to the building; it is the foundation of it. Nehemiah will plan brilliantly, but he will never plan first.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus also wept over Jerusalem, and for the opposite reason: Nehemiah wept because its walls were down, and Jesus wept because he knew they would come down again: they will not leave one stone upon another (Luke 19:41-44).

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now it happened in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel, that Hanani, one of my brothers, came with certain men from Judah. And I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is, for most of its length, a memoir written in the first person: I asked, I sat down, I was cupbearer. We are hearing the man himself.

The date is the month of Chislev, November into December, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I, about 445 BC. The place is Susa the citadel, the winter palace of the Persian kings. It is the same address as the book of Esther (Esth 1:2), where a Jewish girl had become queen a generation earlier under this king's father. God's people had friends in that palace before, and he had put them there.

Nehemiah was very likely born in exile and had never seen Jerusalem. He had a post at the centre of the most powerful court on earth, and no personal need of that ruined city at all. Then his brother Hanani (he calls him my brother Hanani again at 7:2) arrives with men from Judah, and the first thing Nehemiah does in his own book is ask a question.

He asked about the people first and the place second. And he asked at all. A comfortable man can go a long time without asking how things are with the people of God, because the answer might cost him something. Nehemiah wanted to know.
verseByVerse.note: Chislev is November–December. The twentieth year of Artaxerxes I was 445 BC. Susa was the Persian winter capital.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to me, "The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An ancient city without a wall was hardly a city. Anyone could walk in at night; traders would not risk their goods there, and nobody of means would live there. The temple stood on its hill, rebuilt seventy years before, in the middle of a settlement that could not shut a door.

Which ruin is meant is not certain. The walls had been down since 586 BC, and some think Hanani means that old desolation. But under this same Artaxerxes the Jews had begun rebuilding the walls, their neighbours wrote to the king, and his officials by force and power made them cease (Ezra 4:23). A fresh wreck fits a man who sits down and weeps for days far better than a fact everyone had known for a century and a half.

And the word shame will not leave this book. It is the derision Nehemiah means to end at 2:17, the taunt of 4:4, the taunts of the nations at 5:9. The wall is stone and mortar, but it is built against a word: the sneer of neighbours who looked at the ruin and said that the God of Israel could not look after his own.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sat down; the legs went. Then days of weeping and mourning, and then fasting and prayer. How long is shown by the next date in the book: this is Chislev, and Nehemiah speaks to the king in Nisan (2:1). Four months. The man who will get a wall built in fifty-two days spends more than twice that long on his knees before he lays a stone.

The God of heaven is the title Cyrus used in his decree (Ezra 1:2), the name of God as he stood over an empire. Nehemiah is praying from inside the court of the King of kings of Persia, to the God who reigns over the one he serves.

Nehemiah was safe, well fed and well placed, and the ruin was months of travel away. It cost him four months of grief because it was God's city and God's people, and their shame was God's shame. What does the state of the church cost you: a congregation dwindling, a family that has walked away from the faith? Nehemiah shows what to do with that grief. Do not bury it, and do not rush past it into a plan. Take it before the God of heaven, who has bound himself by covenant to his people, and keep taking it until he opens a door; when we do not know how to pray, the Spirit helps us in our weakness (Rom 8:26).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer says who God is (v. 5), asks him to listen and confesses the nation's sin as Nehemiah's own (vv. 6-7), holds God to his word through Moses (vv. 8-9), pleads that the people are his redeemed (v. 10), and asks for mercy before the king (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Nearly every line of this prayer is borrowed. Its first sentence is Daniel's, its request to be heard is Solomon's, its promise is Moses' in Deuteronomy, and its plea for the people is the argument Moses used after the golden calf. Nehemiah prays in the language God has already used, which is why he can pray it with confidence.
verseByVerse.examples: The book begins with Nehemiah asking God to remember the word (v. 8) and ends with him asking God to remember me, O my God, for good (13:31). Everything between is a man working inside a promise and trusting God to keep the account.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said, "O LORD God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he says a word about Jerusalem, he says who God is, and the words are Daniel's, almost exactly (Dan 9:4). Daniel prayed them in Babylon about ninety-four years before, when he read in Jeremiah that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years (Dan 9:2), and God answered him with the decree of Cyrus. Now the temple was standing and the walls were not, and Nehemiah picks up Daniel's prayer where Daniel left it.

Daniel had it in turn from Moses (Deut 7:9). Covenant is the promise God has bound himself to; steadfast love, hesed, is the loyalty behind the promise, the love that keeps coming back. But the sentence carries a condition: he keeps covenant with those who love him and keep his commandments. The next two verses will confess that Israel had not. The prayer's first sentence has already named the problem it has to solve.

verseByVerse.quote: let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned. We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The request to be heard is Solomon's language at the dedication of the temple: let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place (2 Chr 6:40). Solomon asked God to listen to prayers made toward that house when his people sinned. Nehemiah is making one.

Listen to the pronouns: the people of Israel, then we, then I and my father's house. He does not stand at a distance and describe the nation's failures to God. He puts himself and his family inside the guilt. He was born long after the exile began; he could have said they. He never does.

A question a reader can put to himself: when you pray about what is wrong in the church, is the subject of the sentence they or we? Nehemiah's we was honest, for he was a sinner himself, and his confession was shared guilt. There is one Intercessor who could have said they truthfully and still took the sin as though it were his: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, 'If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples, but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is not one verse of Moses but the gist of several: the warning of Leviticus 26:33 and Deuteronomy 4:27, the gathering of Deuteronomy 30:4, nearly word for word, and the chosen place of Deuteronomy 12:11. Nehemiah is quoting the whole covenant back to the God who made it.

And look at the logic. The first half of that word had come true to the letter: they had been unfaithful, and they had been scattered, and Nehemiah is praying from Persia to prove it. So the second half is just as sure. The exile was the evidence that God keeps his word. A God who kept the threat will keep the promise.

Unfaithful is the word Leviticus uses for Israel's treachery, and Leviticus had said what should happen next: if they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers ... then I will remember my covenant (Lev 26:40-42). That is exactly the order of this prayer. Nehemiah has confessed, and now he asks God to remember, the first of many times the word appears in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are Moses' words on the worst day in Israel's history. After the golden calf, Moses lay on his face for forty days and argued: do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness (Deut 9:26).

The argument is not that the people deserved better. It is that they belong to God and that he paid for them. Redeemed means bought back. You do not throw away what cost you that much.

That argument is stronger now than when Moses and Nehemiah made it, because the price is greater. You were ransomed ... not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:18-19). Whoever has been bought at that price has an Intercessor who can say to the Father, of the weakest of his people: they are yours, and look what they cost.

verseByVerse.quote: O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man." Now I was cupbearer to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is not alone. Others were praying too, people who delight to fear your name, and he asks God to hear them all together.

Today, because he has picked a day. This man, because the most powerful ruler on earth is, before God, a man.

And this man had put the problem there. Artaxerxes had ordered the building stopped until a decree is made by me (Ezra 4:21). The king had left himself one door, and Nehemiah was praying to walk through it: to ask the emperor to reverse his own order. In Persia, a servant who displeased the king could lose his head.

Only after the prayer do we learn who has been praying. The cupbearer stood within arm's length of the throne, trusted with the king's life. That is the whole chapter in its last line: a man with a broken heart for God's city and access to the king.

We have a greater one. Nehemiah would go in trembling, afraid of the king's face (2:2). Our Intercessor sits at the right hand of the throne: we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, so we may with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:15-16), and he always lives to make intercession for us (Heb 7:25). The cupbearer had to wait four months for his moment. The Son never has to wait at all.
verseByVerse.note: A cupbearer tasted the king’s wine and was a trusted adviser with access to the king.

2.title: Vision in the Dark
2.text: <sup>1</sup>In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad in his presence.<sup>2</sup>And the king said to me, "Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart." Then I was very much afraid.<sup>3</sup>I said to the king, "Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?"<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to me, "What are you requesting?" So I prayed to the God of heaven.<sup>5</sup>And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may rebuild it."<sup>6</sup>And the king said to me (the queen sitting beside him), "How long will you be gone, and when will you return?" So it pleased the king to send me when I had given him a time.<sup>7</sup>And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors of the province Beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah,<sup>8</sup>and a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress of the temple, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall occupy." And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me.<sup>9</sup>Then I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen.<sup>10</sup>But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.<sup>11</sup>So I went to Jerusalem and was there three days.<sup>12</sup>Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me but the one on which I rode.<sup>13</sup>I went out by night by the Valley Gate to the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been destroyed by fire.<sup>14</sup>Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal that was under me to pass.<sup>15</sup>Then I went up in the night by the valley and inspected the wall, and I turned back and entered by the Valley Gate, and so returned.<sup>16</sup>And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, and I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, and the rest who were to do the work.<sup>17</sup>Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision."<sup>18</sup>And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, "Let us rise up and build." So they strengthened their hands for the good work.<sup>19</sup>But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, "What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?"<sup>20</sup>Then I replied to them, "The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem."
2.overview: Four months after the report, Nehemiah's grief shows on his face as he serves the king his wine. Terrified, he speaks of the city of my fathers' graves, never naming Jerusalem to the king who had stopped its building (vv. 1-3). He prays in the moment, asks to be sent, with letters and timber, and the king grants it, for the good hand of my God was upon me (vv. 4-8). He travels with the cavalry escort Ezra had refused, to the displeasure of Sanballat and Tobiah (vv. 9-10), rides the ruins alone at night (vv. 11-16), and calls the leaders to build, telling them of God's hand (vv. 17-18). To the charge of rebellion he answers that the God of heaven will prosper them (vv. 19-20).
2.theology:
God's providence works through a servant's sad face, a king's question, a prayer in a pause, and a practical list of letters and timber. Prayer and planning are not rivals: the man who prayed four months also knew what beams he needed. And the good hand of God rests equally on Ezra, who refused an escort, and on Nehemiah, who accepted one; faith is not a method.

The builder who left a palace for a ruin is a real but limited likeness of Christ, who came without letters or horsemen (Phil 2:7), and who was accused of the same rebellion against the king (John 19:12).
2.examples:
He kept his grief off his face for four months, and then the king noticed.

He never said the word Jerusalem to the king.

He prayed in the pause between a question and an answer.

The timber for the gates came out of the king's own forest.

On the east side the rubble was too thick for his animal to pass.

He had been in the city three days and said the trouble we are in.

His enemies will have no memorial in the city; he asks God to remember him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Good Hand of My God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Nisan the king sees the sadness Nehemiah can no longer hide (vv. 1-3). Asked what he wants, Nehemiah prays, then asks to be sent to rebuild, with letters of passage and timber, and the king grants it (vv. 4-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Four months of prayer, and then the answer came through a slip in a servant's composure that he had not planned and could not have staged. God turned the king's heart (Prov 21:1) by way of Nehemiah's sad face.

verseByVerse.quote: In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad in his presence. And the king said to me, "Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart." Then I was very much afraid. I said to the king, "Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nisan is March into April. Chapter 1 was also dated to the twentieth year, in Chislev; Nehemiah apparently counts the king's years from the autumn, so the two dates are four months apart in the same regnal year.

For four months he had carried the grief and kept it off his face. A Persian king did not care to see sorrow near him; in the book of Esther no one was allowed to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth (Esth 4:2). Then one day, with the cup in his hand, the mask slipped.

Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart. Then I was very much afraid. The king had seen straight through him. An unhappy servant close to the royal cup could look like a dangerous one.

Nehemiah's own record says plainly that he was terrified. Courage in Scripture is not the absence of fear but doing the next right thing while afraid, leaning on the God who has heard four months of prayer rather than on nerve. A reader shaking at some conversation he knows he has to have is in good company here.

What he does not say matters. He does not say Jerusalem. This king had once been told it was that rebellious and wicked city (Ezra 4:12) and had ordered its building stopped. So Nehemiah speaks of his fathers' graves, a claim any man in any nation would understand, and lets the king reach the name for himself. Truthful, and wise.
verseByVerse.note: Nisan is March–April, four months after Nehemiah first heard the news.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to me, "What are you requesting?" So I prayed to the God of heaven. And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may rebuild it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A king has asked a question and is waiting. There are perhaps three seconds before silence becomes insolence, and into them Nehemiah puts a prayer: no words aloud, no bowed head the king would notice, a cry sent upward between the question and the answer.

That kind of prayer does not come from nowhere. The long prayer made the short one possible; the habit made the reflex. In the pause before you answer a hard question at work or at home, is the God of heaven the first one you turn to? The remedy is not a technique for that moment but the months before it, and the Spirit by whom God's children cry to their Father is given for moments like this (Rom 8:15).

The request is enormous: send the king's own cupbearer to rebuild the city the king had forbidden to be rebuilt. And he still has not named it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to me (the queen sitting beside him), "How long will you be gone, and when will you return?" So it pleased the king to send me when I had given him a time. And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors of the province Beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah, and a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress of the temple, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall occupy." And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen beside the king is an eyewitness's detail; he remembered who was in the room. And the question is already a yes: not whether, but when. In the end he governed Judah for twelve years (5:14) before returning to the king (13:6).

Then the petition turns practical: letters to the governors Beyond the River for safe passage, and a letter to the keeper of the king's forest for beams for the gates, the wall and his own house. He had spent four months praying, and also thinking. Prayer and planning were never rivals in this man.

The word for the king's forest, pardes, is the Persian word for a royal park that has given us our word paradise. The timber for Jerusalem's gates came out of the king's paradise.

That is Ezra's sentence. Of Ezra it was written that the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him (Ezra 7:6), and the good hand of his God was on him (7:9). Thirteen years later the same hand rests on the second man. The king did the granting. God's hand is the reason he did.

Many Christian interpreters have also counted Daniel's seventy weeks from a word to restore and build Jerusalem (Dan 9:25) to the coming of the Messiah, starting either from this commission in about 445 BC or from Ezra's in about 458. The calculations differ, and faithful Christians hold them with an open hand; what is not in doubt is that the city rebuilt under these decrees was the one into which the Anointed One came.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — Let Us Rise Up and Build
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nehemiah arrives with the king's letters and a cavalry escort, and Sanballat and Tobiah are greatly displeased that someone has come to seek Israel's welfare (vv. 9-10). After three days and a night ride round the ruins, telling no one (vv. 11-16), he calls the leaders to build so that they may no longer suffer derision, tells them of God's hand, and they agree (vv. 17-18). To the jeer of rebellion he answers in God's name that the enemies have no claim in Jerusalem (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter's word is good: God's good hand (v. 8), the good of Israel that the enemy resents (v. 10), the hand upon him for good and the good work (v. 18). The book will end on it: Remember me, O my God, for good (13:31).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen. But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put that beside Ezra. Thirteen years earlier Ezra had made the same journey and was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen (Ezra 8:22), because he had told the king that God protects those who seek him. Nehemiah rides in with cavalry. Both men had the good hand of God upon them.

So neither is a rule. There are times when faith refuses the means on offer, so that everyone will see that God did it, and times when it accepts them with thanks, because God provided them. The same God was with the man who went without a guard and the man who went with one.

Sanballat was governor of Samaria, to the north; Tobiah was an official in Ammon, across the Jordan, with friends inside Jerusalem (6:17-19). A weak Jerusalem suited them both. Their complaint is the most honest thing they say in the whole book: someone had come to do these people good.
verseByVerse.note: Sanballat was governor of Samaria; Tobiah, an official in Ammon.

verseByVerse.quote: So I went to Jerusalem and was there three days. Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me but the one on which I rode. I went out by night by the Valley Gate to the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been destroyed by fire. Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal that was under me to pass. Then I went up in the night by the valley and inspected the wall, and I turned back and entered by the Valley Gate, and so returned. And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, and I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, and the rest who were to do the work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days first, as Ezra had done on arriving (Ezra 8:32). A man coming off a journey of months does not start a revolution on the first morning.

The plan was God's, put into my heart, and he kept it to himself. Tobiah had friends in the city, and a plan announced before it is ready is a plan handed to the opposition.

The ride runs out by the Valley Gate on the west, down to the Dragon Spring and the Dung Gate at the southern tip, round to the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool. There, on the steep eastern slope, the old wall and terraces had tumbled into the valley in heaps too choked for his animal to pick through, so he went up the valley looking at the wall from below, and came back in by the gate he had left by.

A man walking in the dark along a ruin, touching the burned timber, measuring the size of the problem alone before he asks anyone else to lift a stone. He would not call people to a work he had not seen with his own eyes. And though nobody yet knew what he was doing, he already calls them the rest who were to do the work.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision." And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, "Let us rise up and build." So they strengthened their hands for the good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trouble we are in. He had lived in the city three days. He could have said you. He said we, as he had said it in his prayer (1:6). And at last he names the city: Jerusalem, twice. Derision is the shame Hanani reported in 1:3: the neighbours' sneer, which a wall would silence.

Testimony first. He did not begin with a plan or a rota. He told them what God had done, and then what the king had said. The people of Jerusalem had watched the last attempt at a wall pulled down by force; what could make them try again was the news that God had moved.

So they strengthened their hands for the good work. The enemy hated the good; God's hand was for it; the people put their hands to it. When Nehemiah's last recorded words ask God to remember him for good, he is asking to be counted in with this.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, "What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?" Then I replied to them, "The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there are three: Sanballat from Samaria to the north, Tobiah from Ammon to the east, Geshem the Arab from the desert to the south. Their first weapon is a laugh, then the old charge of rebellion, which had stopped the wall before (Ezra 4:12-16). This time it was absurd, with the king's letters in Nehemiah's baggage. But it is the charge the world reaches for whenever God's people build, and it crucified the Son of God: Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar (John 19:12).

He had the king's letters and did not wave them. He answered in God's name. The last word, claim, may be rendered "memorial", as the ESV's note says: Sanballat and his friends will have no memorial in Jerusalem, and the man who says so will end his book asking God to remember him.

Nehemiah left a palace to live among ruins and derision because he loved God's people. The likeness to Christ is real, and so is its limit. Nehemiah went with letters and horsemen. The Son of God emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant (Phil 2:7), and came with neither, into a far greater ruin, to build a city whose enemies will have no memorial in it at all.

3.title: Every Hand on the Wall

3.overview: A register of the builders, section by section, beginning with Eliashib the high priest at the Sheep Gate (v. 1) and going anticlockwise round the whole city until the goldsmiths and merchants close the circuit there (v. 32). Priests and Levites, townsmen from Jericho to Tekoa, goldsmiths and perfumers, rulers, temple servants and merchants all take a stretch; Shallum builds he and his daughters (v. 12). Only the nobles of Tekoa hold back (v. 5), and Meremoth, of a priestly family once excluded for want of a genealogy (Ezra 2:61-62), builds twice (vv. 4, 21).
3.theology:
No section of this wall is anyone's own work: thirty-one times the text says next to him or after him. The people of God are built together, and God keeps the names of those who work (Heb 6:10).

The Tower of Hananel (v. 1) and the Horse Gate (v. 28) are the two landmarks of Jeremiah's promise that the city would be rebuilt for the LORD, given in the same chapter as the new covenant (Jer 31:31-40). Nehemiah's wall was an instalment. The city that will not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever is the one John saw, with names inscribed on its gates and foundations (Rev 21:12-14).
3.examples:
The high priest laid the first stones; his grandson married Sanballat's daughter.

A priest from a family once barred for want of a genealogy built two sections.

The nobles of Tekoa would not bend their necks; the men of Tekoa did two stretches.

Descendants of the Gibeonites who tricked Joshua built Jerusalem's wall.

Goldsmiths and perfumers lifted stone.

Shallum's daughters are the only women mentioned on the wall.

A district ruler took the Dung Gate.

Men built opposite their own houses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — They Built the Sheep Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest and the priests build the Sheep Gate (v. 1), and the work runs along the north wall, where only the nobles of Tekoa refuse (vv. 2-5), down the west side with goldsmiths, perfumers and rulers, and Shallum with his daughters (vv. 6-12), and round the southern gates (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Thirty-one times the chapter says next to him or after him. No section is anybody's own achievement; every stretch of wall joins someone else's.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brothers the priests, and they built the Sheep Gate. They consecrated it and set its doors. They consecrated it as far as the Tower of the Hundred, as far as the Tower of Hananel. And next to him the men of Jericho built. And next to them Zaccur the son of Imri built.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This chapter is a list, and it should be read as one: Nehemiah's work sheet, going anticlockwise round the city from the temple corner until it arrives back where it began. But nobody keeps a record like this unless every name on it mattered.

The first man on the wall is the most senior man in Israel's religion, with his hands on the stones. He begins at the Sheep Gate, through which the flocks came in for the sacrifices, the only gate in the list that is consecrated. Nearly five centuries later there was a pool by the Sheep Gate where Jesus told a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years to get up and walk (John 5:2-8).

Hold one fact about Eliashib for later. In chapter 13 his grandson is married to the daughter of Sanballat (13:28), and an Eliashib, probably this one, has given Tobiah a room in the temple (13:4-7). The man who built the first gate let the enemy in through his own family. A good start is not the same as a faithful finish.

The Tower of Hananel: remember that name; it appears in a promise of Jeremiah's that this chapter begins to keep. And next to him the men of Jericho built: the city whose walls fell flat when Israel first entered the land sends men to put up Jerusalem's.
verseByVerse.note: The Sheep Gate stood near the temple; Jesus healed a man at the pool by it.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate. They laid its beams and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And next to them Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz repaired. And next to them Meshullam the son of Berechiah, son of Meshezabel repaired. And next to them Zadok the son of Baana repaired. And next to them the Tekoites repaired, but their nobles would not stoop to serve their Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hakkoz. When the exiles first came home, the family of Hakkoz could not find its name in the genealogies and was excluded from the priesthood as unclean (Ezra 2:61-62). Eighty years later Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, is the priest into whose hands Ezra weighed the temple's silver and gold (Ezra 8:33), and here he builds two sections (v. 21). The family that nearly lost its place gave more than almost anyone.

Tekoa was a hill town some ten miles south, the town of Amos (Amos 1:1). Its ordinary men came in and worked. Its great men would not bend their necks to it, like an ox that will not take the yoke. The Tekoites answered by doing a second section (v. 27).

There is a yoke that is offered to every proud neck, and it is not heavy: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29). The one who says it stooped lower than any noble of Tekoa was ever asked to.

verseByVerse.quote: Joiada the son of Paseah and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah repaired the Gate of Yeshanah. They laid its beams and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And next to them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon and of Mizpah, the seat of the governor of the province Beyond the River. Next to them Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, goldsmiths, repaired. Next to him Hananiah, one of the perfumers, repaired, and they restored Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall. Next to them Rephaiah the son of Hur, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired. Next to them Jedaiah the son of Harumaph repaired opposite his house. And next to him Hattush the son of Hashabneiah repaired. Malchijah the son of Harim and Hasshub the son of Pahath-moab repaired another section and the Tower of the Ovens. Next to him Shallum the son of Hallohesh, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired, he and his daughters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Round the north-west corner and down the western side the names keep coming. Melatiah the Gibeonite and the men of Gibeon: descendants of the Canaanites who tricked Joshua and were made cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD (Josh 9:27). The outsiders who were made servants of the altar are building its city's wall.

Goldsmiths and a perfumer, men with soft hands, lift rough stone. Two rulers of half the district of Jerusalem take sections (vv. 9, 12), and Jedaiah builds opposite his house (v. 10), the first of several who built the stretch they would sleep behind.

Shallum's daughters are the only women mentioned on the wall. Their names are not given and nothing else is known of them. They carried stone beside their father, and Scripture kept the fact.

That is what the list is for. God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name (Heb 6:10). Most of the work done for God in any generation is done by people whose names are forgotten within fifty years. Not one of them is forgotten by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate. They rebuilt it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars, and repaired a thousand cubits of the wall, as far as the Dung Gate. Malchijah the son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem, repaired the Dung Gate. He rebuilt it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And Shallum the son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt it and covered it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And he built the wall of the Pool of Shelah of the king's garden, as far as the stairs that go down from the city of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hanun and the men of Zanoah rebuild the Valley Gate and a thousand cubits of wall, about five hundred yards, the only stretch in the chapter given a length, and a long one. Perhaps the wall there needed less, perhaps Zanoah simply sent many men.

The Dung Gate was the gate through which the city's refuse went out to the valley, and a district ruler took it. Set him beside the nobles of Tekoa, who would not bend their necks at all.

Shelah is the pool Isaiah called Shiloah, the waters of Shiloah that flow gently (Isa 8:6), the pool the Gospels call Siloam, where Jesus sent a blind man to wash, and he came back seeing (John 9:7).
verseByVerse.note: The Pool of Shelah is probably the Pool of Siloam.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–32 — Each Opposite His Own House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Up the eastern side: Levites, rulers, householders opposite their own houses, Meremoth again past the high priest's house, the temple servants by the Water Gate, the Tekoites again, and the priests above the Horse Gate, until the circuit closes at the Sheep Gate (vv. 16-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven times a man or a group repairs another section, a second stretch after finishing a first. Nobody was forced to; they saw a gap and filled it. Several build the wall in front of their own door.

verseByVerse.quote: After him Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, repaired to a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the artificial pool, and as far as the house of the mighty men. After him the Levites repaired: Rehum the son of Bani. Next to him Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, repaired for his district. After him their brothers repaired: Bavvai the son of Henadad, ruler of half the district of Keilah. Next to him Ezer the son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section opposite the ascent to the armory at the buttress. After him Baruch the son of Zabbai repaired another section from the buttress to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest. After him Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz repaired another section from the door of the house of Eliashib to the end of the house of Eliashib. After him the priests, the men of the surrounding area, repaired. After them Benjamin and Hasshub repaired opposite their house. After them Azariah the son of Maaseiah, son of Ananiah repaired beside his own house. After him Binnui the son of Henadad repaired another section, from the house of Azariah to the buttress and to the corner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Nehemiah, son of Azbuk and ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, is not the governor telling the story. He worked near the tombs of David, the royal burial place inside the old city.

Then Baruch builds to the door of the high priest's house, and Meremoth of the family of Hakkoz does his second stretch along it (vv. 20-21). The house was large enough to take a section of wall to itself, and the man from the family once shut out of the priesthood built in front of it.

Nehemiah seems to have assigned men where they lived when he could. A man builds carefully when his own children sleep on the other side of the stones.

verseByVerse.quote: Palal the son of Uzai repaired opposite the buttress and the tower projecting from the upper house of the king at the court of the guard. After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh and the temple servants living on Ophel repaired to a point opposite the Water Gate on the east and the projecting tower. After him the Tekoites repaired another section opposite the great projecting tower as far as the wall of Ophel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The court of the guard was where Jeremiah had been held prisoner while the Babylonians besieged the city (Jer 32:2), and where he bought a field, because God had told him that houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (Jer 32:15). On the same spot, a century and a half later, men of that land are building.

The temple servants who lived on Ophel, the ridge south of the temple, work opposite the Water Gate. It is in the square before that gate that the whole people will gather to hear Ezra read the law (8:1). And the Tekoites repair another section: their nobles had done nothing; the men of Tekoa did two.

verseByVerse.quote: Above the Horse Gate the priests repaired, each one opposite his own house. After them Zadok the son of Immer repaired opposite his own house. After him Shemaiah the son of Shecaniah, the keeper of the East Gate, repaired. After him Hananiah the son of Shelemiah and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph repaired another section. After him Meshullam the son of Berechiah repaired opposite his chamber. After him Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths, repaired as far as the house of the temple servants and of the merchants, opposite the Muster Gate, and to the upper chamber of the corner. And between the upper chamber of the corner and the Sheep Gate the goldsmiths and the merchants repaired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set this chapter beside a promise. In the chapter in which Jeremiah announced the new covenant (Jer 31:33), he added that the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the Tower of Hananel to the corner of the Horse Gate, and shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever (Jer 31:38-40). The Tower of Hananel is in verse 1 of this chapter; the Horse Gate is in verse 28. The people with their trowels were walking the line of Jeremiah's promise.

And yet not the whole of it. Jerusalem's walls came down again under Rome. The city that will never be plucked up is still to come, and when John saw it, its gates and foundations bore the names of the twelve tribes and of the twelve apostles of the Lamb (Rev 21:12, 14). The God who had the name of every builder on Nehemiah's wall written down builds his last city with names on its stones. And the Lamb whose apostles are written there is the one every sheep through that first gate had been pointing to.

4.title: Trowel and Sword
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews.<sup>2</sup>And he said in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria, "What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore it for themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish up in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that?"<sup>3</sup>Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, "Yes, what they are building— if a fox goes up on it he will break down their stone wall!"<sup>4</sup>Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads and give them up to be plundered in a land where they are captives.<sup>5</sup>Do not cover their guilt, and let not their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders.<sup>6</sup>So we built the wall. And all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.<sup>7</sup>But when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem was going forward and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were very angry.<sup>8</sup>And they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it.<sup>9</sup>And we prayed to our God and set a guard as a protection against them day and night.<sup>10</sup>In Judah it was said, "The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. There is too much rubble. By ourselves we will not be able to rebuild the wall."<sup>11</sup>And our enemies said, "They will not know or see till we come among them and kill them and stop the work."<sup>12</sup>At that time the Jews who lived near them came from all directions and said to us ten times, "You must return to us."<sup>13</sup>So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in open places, I stationed the people by their clans, with their swords, their spears, and their bows.<sup>14</sup>And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes."<sup>15</sup>When our enemies heard that it was known to us and that God had frustrated their plan, we all returned to the wall, each to his work.<sup>16</sup>From that day on, half of my servants worked on construction, and half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail. And the leaders stood behind the whole house of Judah,<sup>17</sup>who were building on the wall. Those who carried burdens were loaded in such a way that each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other.<sup>18</sup>And each of the builders had his sword strapped at his side while he built. The man who sounded the trumpet was beside me.<sup>19</sup>And I said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "The work is great and widely spread, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another.<sup>20</sup>In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us."<sup>21</sup>So we labored at the work, and half of them held the spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out.<sup>22</sup>I also said to the people at that time, "Let every man and his servant pass the night within Jerusalem, that they may be a guard for us by night and may labor by day."<sup>23</sup>So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the men of the guard who followed me, none of us took off our clothes; each kept his weapon at his right hand.
4.overview: Sanballat mocks the feeble Jews before the army of Samaria, and Tobiah says a fox could knock their wall down (vv. 1-3). Nehemiah prays God to turn the taunt back on them, in words borrowed from Jeremiah (vv. 4-5), and the wall rises to half its height, for the people had a mind to work (v. 6). The enemies, now on every side, plot an attack; the people pray and set a guard (vv. 7-9); but the burden-bearers are exhausted and relatives beg the men to come home (vv. 10-12). Nehemiah posts the families at the weak points and tells them to remember the Lord and fight (vv. 13-14). God frustrates the plan, and from then on they build with one hand and hold a weapon with the other, trusting that Our God will fight for us (vv. 15-20), and sleep in their clothes (vv. 21-23).
4.theology:
Prayer and prudence are never set against each other in this chapter: we prayed to our God and set a guard. Nor are God's fighting and theirs (vv. 14, 20). The sovereign God works through means, and his people's effort is the form his help takes.

Sanballat's scornful question — can burned stones be made alive? — is answered in Christ, the living stone rejected by men, who makes dead people into living stones built into God's house (1 Pet 2:4-5). And the imprecation of vv. 4-5 is handed to God, never carried out by hand; since the cross the believer's first prayer for an enemy is for his forgiveness (Acts 7:60), leaving justice to God (Rom 12:19).
4.examples:
Sanballat asked whether burned stones could be revived; God builds with nothing else.

Tobiah's fox is kin to the jackals Lamentations saw prowling over ruined Zion.

The discouragement came from inside, at the halfway point.

Their own families told them ten times to come home.

Nehemiah's cure for fear was the first line of his own prayer: great and awesome.

One hand on the work, one on the weapon.

The governor slept in his clothes like everyone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Will They Revive the Stones?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sanballat and Tobiah jeer at the builders before the army of Samaria (vv. 1-3). Nehemiah takes the taunt to God (vv. 4-5), and the wall is joined all round to half its height (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The first weapon is laughter. Nehemiah does not answer it; he takes it to God and goes back to the wall. The best reply to they cannot was a wall at half its height.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews. And he said in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria, "What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore it for themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish up in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that?" Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, "Yes, what they are building— if a fox goes up on it he will break down their stone wall!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He jeers in public, in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria, which means it is meant to be carried back to the builders. Laughter is cheaper than soldiers, and sometimes it works as well.

What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore it for themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish up in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that? Five questions, each a small dose of doubt. Are you strong enough? Do you think you can pray it up? Do you know how long this will take? And the cleverest one last. Limestone that has been through a fire goes soft and crumbles; stones dug out of burned rubble were close to useless. He was not wrong about the stones.

But look at his verb. Revive means make alive, the word Ezra used when he thanked God for a little reviving (Ezra 9:8). Can dead stones come to life? Sanballat meant it as a joke. It is, in fact, exactly what God does. As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men ... you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house (1 Pet 2:4-5). God builds with burned and broken material; it is the only material he has ever had.

A fox weighs next to nothing. And the fox was the animal of Jerusalem's ruin: Mount Zion which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it (Lam 5:18), in Hebrew the same creature. Tobiah is saying that Zion is still what Lamentations said it was, a place for wild dogs and foxes.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads and give them up to be plundered in a land where they are captives. Do not cover their guilt, and let not their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah does not answer Sanballat. He answers God. Taunt is the word for the shame of 1:3, and he asks God to send it back where it came from. And the second sentence is borrowed from Jeremiah, whose enemies were plotting to kill him: Forgive not their iniquity, nor blot out their sin from your sight (Jer 18:23).

A Christian reading this may be troubled, and should be allowed to ask. How does it sit with Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34)? Three things, plainly. First, Nehemiah takes no revenge; he hands the matter to God, which is exactly what the New Testament commands: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). Second, his reason is not a private insult but that they provoked you to anger — they were setting themselves against God's own work. Third, the cry for justice is not abolished in the New Testament; the martyrs under the altar still pray how long before you will judge and avenge our blood? (Rev 6:10).

But the Christian's first prayer for an enemy is now Stephen's: Lord, do not hold this sin against them (Acts 7:60). If someone has wronged you badly, you may tell God the whole of it and ask him to deal justly. You may not take it into your own hands, and you pray for their repentance before anything else. That is beyond us by nature. It becomes possible because we were God's enemies when Christ died for us (Rom 5:10), and his Spirit teaches us to forgive as we have been forgiven. Justice for the one who never repents is safe with God.

verseByVerse.quote: So we built the wall. And all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we built is the whole of Nehemiah's reply to the five questions and the fox. He prayed, and then he laid the next stone. The separate gangs of chapter 3 had met, and there was now one continuous wall right round the city, at half height.

A mind to work is, literally, a heart to work: the people's hearts were in it. Mockery can take the heart out of a people faster than any army; here it did not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Surrounded enemies plot an attack, and the people pray and set a guard (vv. 7-9). Inside Judah the workers are spent and families urge their men home (vv. 10-12). Nehemiah posts the people by clans and calls them to remember the Lord and fight for their homes (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The cure Nehemiah gives for fear is a memory. The words great and awesome are the first words of his own prayer in 1:5. What he had said to God, he now says to the people.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem was going forward and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were very angry. And they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it. And we prayed to our God and set a guard as a protection against them day and night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at the map: Samaria to the north, the Ammonites to the east, the Arabs to the south, and now the Ashdodites from the old Philistine coast to the west. In chapter 2 there were three enemies; now Jerusalem is surrounded. The laughter stopped when the gaps began to close, and the plotting began.

Prayer and a guard, both. They did not pray instead of posting sentries, and they did not post sentries instead of praying. Faith that refuses to lock the door is presumption, and a locked door without prayer is not safety.

verseByVerse.quote: In Judah it was said, "The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. There is too much rubble. By ourselves we will not be able to rebuild the wall." And our enemies said, "They will not know or see till we come among them and kill them and stop the work." At that time the Jews who lived near them came from all directions and said to us ten times, "You must return to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This time the voice is not Sanballat's but Judah's own, and it has turned into a lament. The men carrying earth and stone up the slope were spent, and the heaps of rubble never seemed to get smaller.

It came straight after half its height. The start of a great work has its own energy, and the end has the finish line in sight; the middle is where the strength goes. Many readers are at a halfway point just now, a marriage in its hard years, a long illness, a work for God with no end in sight, and know this sentence from the inside. By ourselves we will not be able. That is true. It was never meant to be done by themselves. To the builders of the temple a lifetime before, God had said, Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zech 4:6), and that Spirit now lives in his people.

Then the enemy boasts of a surprise attack (v. 11), and Jews from the villages near the enemy urge their families ten times, over and over, to come home (the Hebrew of verse 12 is hard, and the KJV reads it as a warning that the enemy would come from every side). The hardest pressure to go back often comes from people who love you.

verseByVerse.quote: So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in open places, I stationed the people by their clans, with their swords, their spears, and their bows. And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He put the people where the wall was lowest and where the enemy could see them, and he put them there by families. A man stands his ground when his own brothers are beside him.

Great and awesome are the first words of Nehemiah's prayer in Susa (1:5). Months of praying had put them into his mouth, and now he gives them to the people. The cure for fear is not a better estimate of the enemy but a memory of God: fear grows when the enemy fills the whole view, and shrinks when the Lord is remembered for what he is.

And then, fight. Remembering God did not make the fighting unnecessary. It made it possible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Our God Will Fight for Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God frustrates the plan and the people return to the work (v. 15). From then on half work and half stand armed, every builder with a sword, and the trumpet ready to rally them, for God will fight for them (vv. 16-20). They work from dawn till the stars come out and never take off their clothes (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Fight for your brothers (v. 14) and our God will fight for us (v. 20) in the same speech. Moses had said the second at the Red Sea (Exod 14:14). God's fighting did not make theirs unnecessary; theirs did not make his unnecessary.

verseByVerse.quote: When our enemies heard that it was known to us and that God had frustrated their plan, we all returned to the wall, each to his work. From that day on, half of my servants worked on construction, and half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail. And the leaders stood behind the whole house of Judah, who were building on the wall. Those who carried burdens were loaded in such a way that each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other. And each of the builders had his sword strapped at his side while he built. The man who sounded the trumpet was beside me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The surprise attack depended on surprise, and it was lost. Nehemiah credits the whole thing to God, and the result is not a celebration but a return to work, each to his work, back to the particular stretch of wall that was his.

It is a true picture of God's people in this world, and it needs one correction before it is used. The church is not given a literal sword: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4). Its sword is the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph 6:17). But the posture is the same. We build, and we guard what we build, and we never get a season in which only one of those is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "The work is great and widely spread, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another. In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us." So we labored at the work, and half of them held the spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out. I also said to the people at that time, "Let every man and his servant pass the night within Jerusalem, that they may be a guard for us by night and may labor by day." So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the men of the guard who followed me, none of us took off our clothes; each kept his weapon at his right hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our God will fight for us is what Moses said at the Red Sea (Exod 14:14). Yet six verses earlier Nehemiah told these same men to fight (v. 14). God fights, and his people fight, and when they win it is still God's victory.

Everyone slept inside the city so there would be guards by night and workers by day (v. 22), and the governor slept in his clothes with his weapon beside him, like every other man on the wall. (The last words of verse 23 are obscure in Hebrew: the ESV reads that each kept his weapon at his right hand, the KJV that they put off their clothes only for washing.)

That is a leader who asks nothing he does not do. Ours went further. He did not only share his people's watch; he took on himself the attack they could not survive, and won it alone. If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom 8:31).

5.title: The Enemy Within

So let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive."<sup>3</sup>There were also those who said, "We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain because of the famine."<sup>4</sup>And there were those who said, "We have borrowed money for the king's tax on our fields and our vineyards.<sup>5</sup>Now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children are as their children.
