Let us abandon this exacting of interest.<sup>11</sup>Return to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive orchards, and their houses, and the percentage of money, grain, wine, and oil that you have been exacting from them."<sup>12</sup>Then they said, "We will restore these and require nothing from them. We will do as you say." And I called the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised.<sup>13</sup>I also shook out the fold of my garment and said, "So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this promise. So may he be shaken out and emptied." And all the assembly said "Amen" and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.<sup>14</sup>Moreover, from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, twelve years, neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowance of the governor.<sup>15</sup>The former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people and took from them for their daily ration forty shekels of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God.<sup>16</sup>I also persevered in the work on this wall, and we acquired no land, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.<sup>17</sup>Moreover, there were at my table 150 men, Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the nations that were around us.<sup>18</sup>Now what was prepared at my expense for each day was one ox and six choice sheep and birds, and every ten days all kinds of wine in abundance. Yet for all this I did not demand the food allowance of the governor, because the service was too heavy on this people.<sup>19</sup>Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.
5.overview: With the wall half-built, a great outcry rises against the Jews' own nobles: families hungry, fields mortgaged in a famine, money borrowed for the king's tax, and children sold to pay the lenders (vv. 1-5). Nehemiah, very angry, thinks it through and publicly charges the nobles with exacting interest from their brothers (vv. 6-8). He calls them to the fear of our God, the phrase of the interest law itself (Lev 25:36), and, including his own household, demands everything returned that day (vv. 9-11). They swear before the priests, and the assembly says Amen and praises the LORD (vv. 12-13). For twelve years as governor Nehemiah took no allowance, bought no land, and fed 150 men a day from his own purse, and he asks God to remember it (vv. 14-19).
5.theology:
How God's people handle money among themselves is covenant faithfulness, not a side issue. The law forbade interest from a poor brother because God had brought them all out of slavery (Lev 25:36-42); to re-enslave a brother was to undo the Exodus. And a leader's authority to call others to that standard rests on his own practice: Nehemiah demanded the fear of God and had lived by it for twelve years.

The rulers of the nations lord it over their people; Nehemiah would not, and Christ, though rich, became poor and gave his life as a ransom for many (Matt 20:25-28; 2 Cor 8:9). Remember me, O my God, for good is the prayer of a servant who knows his record is safe with God and his standing rests on God's steadfast love (13:22).
5.examples:
The loudest cry in the besieged city was against fellow Jews.

First the crop, then the field, then the daughter.

Nehemiah was very angry, and took counsel with himself before he spoke.

We buy our brothers back; you sell them.

He said let us stop: his own household had been lending too.

He shook his pocket out as a curse on anyone who broke the oath.

In twelve years as governor, with famine and taxes pressing, he bought no land.

He fed 150 men a day and never drew his allowance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Let Us Abandon This Exacting of Interest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poor cry out against their Jewish brothers: hunger, mortgaged fields, the king's tax, daughters enslaved (vv. 1-5). Nehemiah charges the nobles with exacting interest, calls them to the fear of God, and demands restitution that very day; they swear, and the assembly praises the LORD (vv. 6-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The most dangerous enemy of this chapter is not Sanballat. It is a brother with a ledger. The law had forbidden interest from a poor brother with the words fear your God (Lev 25:36), and that is exactly the phrase Nehemiah reaches for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there arose a great outcry of the people and of their wives against their Jewish brothers. For there were those who said, "With our sons and our daughters, we are many. So let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive." There were also those who said, "We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain because of the famine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wall is at half height, the enemy is circling, and the loudest cry in Jerusalem is not against Sanballat but against fellow Jews. It echoes Exodus, where God heard their cry because of their taskmasters (Exod 3:7), and the law had joined that cry to money-lending: if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate (Exod 22:27). The people redeemed from taskmasters had taskmasters again, and they were their own brothers.

And of their wives: the women who had to feed the children were crying loudest. A famine had come (v. 3), the king's tax had not stopped for it (v. 4), and the families at the bottom were going under.

The complaints come in a rising order. Let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive: we simply need food. Then, We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses: we are pledging everything we own to eat this year.

verseByVerse.quote: And there were those who said, "We have borrowed money for the king's tax on our fields and our vineyards. Now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children are as their children. Yet we are forcing our sons and our daughters to be slaves, and some of our daughters have already been enslaved, but it is not in our power to help it, for other men have our fields and our vineyards."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persia taxed the land in silver whether the harvest came or not. A farmer with no crop and a tax demand borrowed from whoever had silver, and the ones who had silver were the nobles.

That is the bottom of the spiral: first the crop, then the field, then the child. Our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers: we are the same blood; my child is worth what his child is worth. And there is no way back, because the fields that could have redeemed her belong to someone else now.

Why could an Israelite sell his child at all? The law allowed a family sunk in debt to pay it off in labour, but it hedged that bitter remedy round: a brother was to be treated as a hired worker, not a slave, set free in the seventh year or at the Jubilee, and sent away with gifts (Exod 21:2-11; Lev 25:39-43; Deut 15:12-15). It was a safety net against starvation, not a licence to own people, and it is a world away from the man-stealing Scripture condemns (Exod 21:16; 1 Tim 1:10). The nobles were tearing even that net, using a famine to take the land that was a family's only way back to freedom.

Measure that against the wall going up outside. You can build a magnificent defence round a people and still let them be devoured from inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words. I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles and the officials. I said to them, "You are exacting interest, each from his brother." And I held a great assembly against them and said to them, "We, as far as we are able, have bought back our Jewish brothers who have been sold to the nations, but you even sell your brothers that they may be sold to us!" They were silent and could not find a word to say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was very angry, and the text does not apologise for it; a father selling his daughter to pay interest to a rich Jew ought to make a godly man angry. But I took counsel with myself, literally, his heart deliberated within him. The anger went through his heart before it went through his mouth.

It gives us a test for our own anger. Nehemiah's anger was on someone else's behalf, not his own; it waited until it had thought; and it went straight to the people responsible, openly. Anger on my own account, unthought, and expressed to everyone except the person concerned, has none of the three. None of us manages this by temper or resolve: self-control is the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22-23), and where our anger has wounded, the way back is confession to God and to the one we hurt.

Nehemiah and others had been spending their own silver redeeming Jews sold abroad as slaves, and the nobles were selling Jews into slavery at home, to be bought back again. The law had forbidden it for a reason that goes back to the Exodus: they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves (Lev 25:42). The nobles could not find a word to say.

Is charging interest sin? The law forbade profiting from a poor brother’s distress (Exod 22:25), which is what these nobles were doing, taking fields and children as pledges. It allowed interest in trade (Deut 23:20). Ordinary lending and mortgages are not sin; exploiting the desperate is.

verseByVerse.quote: So I said, "The thing that you are doing is not good. Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God to prevent the taunts of the nations our enemies? Moreover, I and my brothers and my servants are lending them money and grain. Let us abandon this exacting of interest. Return to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive orchards, and their houses, and the percentage of money, grain, wine, and oil that you have been exacting from them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of our God. That phrase is in the very law they were breaking: Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God, that your brother may live beside you (Lev 25:36). Moses had set the fear of God against the moneylender's profit, and Nehemiah simply quotes the reason back.

The taunts of the nations is the word the book began with, the shame of 1:3. The wall was being built to silence the neighbours' sneer, and the nobles were handing it back to them from the inside. What would Sanballat say of a God whose people sold each other's children?

Let us. Nehemiah's own household had been lending too, and he does not exempt it. As in his first prayer (1:6), he puts his own name inside the rebuke.

The percentage is literally "the hundredth", probably one per cent a month. Not a gradual easing: the land back and the interest back, this very day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "We will restore these and require nothing from them. We will do as you say." And I called the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised. I also shook out the fold of my garment and said, "So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this promise. So may he be shaken out and emptied." And all the assembly said "Amen" and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To their great credit, they did not argue. But Nehemiah knew how promises made in a crowded room evaporate on the way home, so he had them swear before the priests.

The fold of a robe was a man's pocket. Nehemiah turned his inside out and shook it empty in front of them: that is what God will do to the house of the man who breaks this oath. Paul made the same gesture at Corinth, when the synagogue turned on him (Acts 18:6).

A debt cancellation ended in worship. When wrong money is given back, God is praised; it is one of the plainest tests of whether a revival is real. And the nobles show the way back for anyone this chapter convicts: not despair, but confession and restitution before a God who forgives. None of us keeps this law of open-handed love perfectly; Christ kept it, and by his obedience the many are made righteous (Rom 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–19 — Because of the Fear of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For twelve years as governor Nehemiah took no allowance, did not lord it over the people, bought no land, and fed 150 men a day at his own expense, because of the fear of God (vv. 14-18). He asks God to remember it (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The first of Nehemiah's four prayers to be remembered (5:19; 13:14, 22, 31). It is not a claim to have earned God's favour; the man who prays it will also ask to be spared according to the greatness of your steadfast love (13:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, twelve years, neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowance of the governor. The former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people and took from them for their daily ration forty shekels of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God. I also persevered in the work on this wall, and we acquired no land, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the same fear he had just demanded of the nobles (v. 9), and he had lived by it for twelve years. And lorded it over is exactly what Jesus said rulers do, while the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (Matt 20:25-28).

In a famine, with families mortgaging their fields, land could be had for almost nothing. The governor bought none. He kept his own servants on the wall, not on estates.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, there were at my table 150 men, Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the nations that were around us. Now what was prepared at my expense for each day was one ox and six choice sheep and birds, and every ten days all kinds of wine in abundance. Yet for all this I did not demand the food allowance of the governor, because the service was too heavy on this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A governor's table was an office of state: officials to feed, envoys from the neighbouring peoples to entertain, an ox and six choice sheep a day. That is a great deal of meat, and Nehemiah paid for it.

The service is the labour on the wall. Men carrying stone all day, with a sword at their side and a famine at home, were not going to be taxed to feed the governor as well.

There is a greater Governor who did far more than decline an allowance. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9). Nehemiah bought back brothers sold to the nations with his silver (v. 8). Christ bought back his people with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reader may wonder whether this prayer is a little self-regarding. It is not a bid for salvation: he will later add spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love (13:22). He knows he will be kept by mercy. What he asks is that the service he gave, unseen and unpaid, not be lost.

He did not publish his twelve years of self-denial to the people or ask them for thanks. He told God. The governor who went without had a Master who would not forget. God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name (Heb 6:10). Nothing given up for his people's sake, in an office or a kitchen or a hospital corridor, goes unrecorded.

6.title: Finished
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Sanballat and Tobiah and Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that there was no breach left in it (although up to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates),<sup>2</sup>Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono." But they intended to do me harm.<sup>3</sup>And I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?"<sup>4</sup>And they sent to me four times in this way, and I answered them in the same manner.<sup>5</sup>In the same way Sanballat for the fifth time sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand.<sup>6</sup>In it was written, "It is reported among the nations, and Geshem also says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports you wish to become their king.<sup>7</sup>And you have also set up prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, 'There is a king in Judah.' And now the king will hear of these reports. So now come and let us take counsel together."<sup>8</sup>Then I sent to him, saying, "No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind."<sup>9</sup>For they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done." But now, O God, strengthen my hands.<sup>10</sup>Now when I went into the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home, he said, "Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple. Let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you by night."<sup>11</sup>But I said, "Should such a man as I run away? And what man such as I could go into the temple and live? I will not go in."<sup>12</sup>And I understood and saw that God had not sent him, but he had pronounced the prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.<sup>13</sup>For this purpose he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin, and so they could give me a bad name in order to taunt me.<sup>14</sup>Remember Tobiah and Sanballat, O my God, according to these things that they did, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who wanted to make me afraid.<sup>15</sup>So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days.<sup>16</sup>And when all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and fell greatly in their own esteem, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.<sup>17</sup>Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters came to them.<sup>18</sup>For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah: and his son Jehohanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah as his wife.<sup>19</sup>Also they spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to make me afraid.
6.overview: With the wall complete but the doors not yet hung, the enemies turn on Nehemiah himself. Four times Sanballat and Geshem invite him to a meeting at Ono, meaning him harm, and four times he answers that he is doing a great work and cannot come down (vv. 1-4). An open letter accuses him of plotting kingship; he denies it in one sentence and prays for strength (vv. 5-9). A hired prophet urges him to hide in the temple; he refuses to run or to enter where a layman may not go (vv. 10-14). The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the nations see that it was done with the help of our God (vv. 15-16). But Tobiah has marriage ties with leading Jewish families, and his letters keep coming (vv. 17-19).
6.theology:
God's work is finished by God's help, and even his enemies are made to see it (v. 16; Ps 126:2). A word that urges sin for safety's sake is not from God, however it is dressed (v. 12; 1 John 4:1).

The slander that Nehemiah meant to be king was false; the promise behind it was not. Zechariah had announced to Jerusalem that her King was coming (Zech 9:9), and he came, and died under the charge Sanballat invented: the King of the Jews (John 19:19). He is the builder whose city has no enemy inside its walls (Rev 21:27).
6.examples:
I am doing a great work and I cannot come down, four times.

The fifth letter was open, so the slander was published before it was answered.

He answered a long lie with a single sentence.

The prophet told him to hide in the holy place; he would not buy safety with a sin.

The enemies set out to make him afraid, and ended up afraid themselves.

Fifty-two days.

A man who built two sections of the wall had married his daughter into Tobiah's family.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — I Am Doing a Great Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wall is up with no breach left, though the doors are not yet hung (v. 1). Sanballat and Geshem try to lure Nehemiah to a meeting in the plain of Ono, meaning him harm, and four times he gives the same answer (vv. 2-4). A fifth message, an open letter, accuses him of plotting rebellion and kingship, with prophets proclaiming a king in Judah (vv. 5-7). He denies it in one sentence, and asks God to strengthen his hands (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: When the wall could not be stopped, the enemy aimed at the man: first his time, then his reputation. Nehemiah gave neither up. He declined the meeting, denied the lie in one sentence, and prayed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Sanballat and Tobiah and Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that there was no breach left in it (although up to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates), Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono." But they intended to do me harm. And I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?" And they sent to me four times in this way, and I answered them in the same manner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The circle is closed; only the gates stand open, waiting for their doors. Everything the enemy has tried has failed, so the enemy changes target. If the wall cannot be stopped, perhaps the builder can.

Ono lay out in the lowlands toward the coast, a long day's ride from Jerusalem, on neutral ground. It sounded like diplomacy. It was a trap, and Nehemiah knew it.

Ono was literally down, off the hills, but the words carry more than geography. The work was great because it was God's, and a man given a great work cannot spend his days in meetings with people who want it to fail.

Four times the same invitation; four times the same answer. Persistence is the enemy's method, and it works on most of us: the fourth request feels unreasonable to refuse. Which of the invitations crowding your own calendar would take you off the wall God has given you? Not everything that asks for your time is wicked. Some of it is only designed, by someone, to make sure the great work does not get done.
verseByVerse.note: Ono lay in the coastal plain, some twenty miles from Jerusalem — far from help.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way Sanballat for the fifth time sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand. In it was written, "It is reported among the nations, and Geshem also says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports you wish to become their king. And you have also set up prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, 'There is a king in Judah.' And now the king will hear of these reports. So now come and let us take counsel together." Then I sent to him, saying, "No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind." For they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done." But now, O God, strengthen my hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An open letter: unsealed, read by the servant who carried it and by anyone else along the road. The slander had been published before Nehemiah read it.

The lie was false about Nehemiah, who never claimed a crown. But it was true about God's promise. A prophet had proclaimed in Jerusalem two generations earlier, Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he (Zech 9:9). There was a King coming to Judah, and when he came, the charge Sanballat invented was nailed over his head: Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews (John 19:19).

One sentence of denial. He did not write a defence or gather testimonials; a man who answers every slander at length has already stopped building. Then the prayer. When he first called them to build, they strengthened their hands for the good work (2:18); now the enemy wants those hands to drop, and he asks God to strengthen them. That is still where strength for God's work comes from, and the New Testament bids tired believers lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees (Heb 12:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — With the Help of Our God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shemaiah, a prophet paid by Tobiah and Sanballat, urges Nehemiah to hide from assassins inside the temple, and he refuses (vv. 10-13); he asks God to remember the false prophets (v. 14). The wall is finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days, and the nations see God's help in it (vv. 15-16). But Tobiah is related by marriage to leading families in Judah, the nobles correspond with him, and his letters keep coming (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The enemies set out to make Nehemiah afraid (vv. 9, 13, 14, 19), and in the end it was the nations who were afraid (v. 16). Those who had laughed at the feeble Jews (4:2) now saw God in the finished wall.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when I went into the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home, he said, "Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple. Let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you by night." But I said, "Should such a man as I run away? And what man such as I could go into the temple and live? I will not go in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third attack comes in a prophet's voice. Shemaiah is a man shut up in his house, perhaps as a sign, and he speaks with urgency and apparent concern: they are coming for you, tonight; come and hide with me in the holy place, and we will bar the doors. It sounds like a friend saving his life.

Two reasons. First, a governor who ran and hid would have told every builder on the wall that the danger was real and the leader was saving himself. Second, Nehemiah was not a priest, and the law said any outsider who comes near shall be put to death (Num 18:7). A king of Judah had once walked in to burn incense and walked out a leper for the rest of his life (2 Chr 26:16-21). Nehemiah would not buy his safety with a sin.
verseByVerse.note: Only priests could enter the temple building; hiding there would have discredited Nehemiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And I understood and saw that God had not sent him, but he had pronounced the prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. For this purpose he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin, and so they could give me a bad name in order to taunt me. Remember Tobiah and Sanballat, O my God, according to these things that they did, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who wanted to make me afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How did he know God had not sent him? Not by some special sense, but because the prophecy told him to break God's law. A word that tells you to sin in order to be safe did not come from God, whoever speaks it and however holy he sounds.

That test is as useful now as then. Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world (1 John 4:1). Counsel that urges you to do what Scripture forbids — to lie a little to protect yourself, to break a vow because the cost has risen, to hide from a duty because someone says God is telling you to — can be answered as Nehemiah answered it: I will not go in.

Taunt again, the word the book began with (1:3). They could not bring shame on the wall, so they tried to bring it on the man.

So Shemaiah was not alone: a prophetess and a group of prophets had the same message, be afraid. Nehemiah does not denounce them in public. He hands them to God, as he did at 4:4-5.

verseByVerse.quote: So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. And when all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and fell greatly in their own esteem, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elul is August into September. Nehemiah had spoken to the king in Nisan (2:1); five months later, after the long road from Susa and a building season under threat, the wall stood all the way round. Fifty-two days, for a work that had failed for years.

Could a wall really go up so fast? Much of it was repair rather than new building: the old foundations and much of the fallen stone were still there, and chapter 3 shows the whole population at work at once, each family on its own short stretch. Many archaeologists also think Nehemiah's circuit was smaller than the city of the kings, enclosing mainly the old City of David and the temple hill. A later Jewish historian gives a much longer period, but the book's own figure is plain, and believable for a people working that hard under threat.

The fear the enemies manufactured came home to them. They wanted to frighten the builders (v. 9) and make Nehemiah afraid (vv. 13, 14, 19), and here it is the nations who are afraid; the men who laughed at the feeble Jews (4:2) looked at the finished wall and saw God in it. It is the song of the returned exiles: then they said among the nations, The LORD has done great things for them (Ps 126:2). God does not need his enemies' approval, but he does sometimes make them his witnesses. Nehemiah does not say that he had managed a remarkable project. He lets the enemies say it was done with the help of our God.
verseByVerse.note: Elul is August–September. The wall took 52 days.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters came to them. For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah: and his son Jehohanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah as his wife. Also they spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to make me afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book does not stop at the triumph, and that is its honesty. While the wall was going up, the nobles were writing to the enemy.

The sons of Arah were a family of the first return (Ezra 2:5). And Meshullam son of Berechiah had built two sections of this wall with his own hands (3:4, 30). He had built against Tobiah by day and married his daughter into Tobiah's family.

Tobiah's friends praised him to Nehemiah's face and carried Nehemiah's words back to him. The wall had closed every gap in the stone, and the enemy walked in through the family.

That is a warning for every work of God. Walls keep out the enemy who attacks; they do nothing against the one you marry into, correspond with, and speak well of. This thread will run to the last chapter, where Tobiah is found living in a room in the temple (13:4-9). The only city whose gates can safely stand open is the one in which nothing unclean will ever enter (Rev 21:27), because its King has dealt with the enemy inside as well as the one outside.

7.overview: The doors are hung, and Nehemiah puts his brother Hanani and the God-fearing Hananiah in charge of Jerusalem, with orders for the gates and the watch (vv. 1-3). But the city is large and nearly empty (v. 4). God puts it into Nehemiah's heart to enrol the people, and he finds the register of those who came up with Zerubbabel ninety years before (v. 5). The register follows (vv. 6-73), almost the same as Ezra 2: leaders, families and towns, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and those whose descent could not be proved. The stated total is 42,360, though the figures sum to 31,089. The chapter ends where Ezra 2 ends and Ezra 3 begins: when the seventh month had come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The City Was Wide and Large
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the doors hung, Nehemiah puts Hanani and Hananiah in charge of Jerusalem, with orders for the gates and the watch (vv. 1-3). The city is large but empty, and God moves him to enrol the people; he finds the register of the first return (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: A wall is not a city. The fifty-two days had produced a perimeter round a place where hardly anyone lived, and the rest of the book is about filling it with a people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the wall had been built and I had set up the doors, and the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites had been appointed, I gave my brother Hanani and Hananiah the governor of the castle charge over Jerusalem, for he was a more faithful and God-fearing man than many. And I said to them, "Let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun is hot. And while they are still standing guard, let them shut and bar the doors. Appoint guards from among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, some at their guard posts and some in front of their own homes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hanani is the brother who brought the news to Susa (1:2). Hananiah, commander of the fortress by the temple, was chosen for his character. Nehemiah does not say he was the most able man, or the best connected, but that he was a more faithful and God-fearing man than many. That is still the first question to ask of anyone given charge of anything in God's house.

The gates stay shut until the sun is hot, well into the morning, when a dawn attack is no longer possible, and the guards are the city's own people, some in front of their own homes. It is the principle of chapter 3 again: a man watches best the street where his children sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: The city was wide and large, but the people within it were few, and no houses had been rebuilt. Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles and the officials and the people to be enrolled by genealogy. And I found the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first, and I found written in it:
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new wall running right round the hills, gates with new doors, and inside, open ground, rubble, a scattering of families, and the temple. The walls had been built for a city that did not yet exist. A church can be like this: a fine building, a well-drawn constitution, and very few people inside who know why they are there.

My God put it into my heart is the phrase he used of the wall itself (2:12). The census was as much from God as the wall. And the first thing he did was look at the past: before he decided who should live in Jerusalem, he reminded himself who God had brought home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–60 — Those Who Came Up at the First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The register of the first return (vv. 6-7): lay families (vv. 8-25), the men of the towns (vv. 26-38), priests (vv. 39-42), Levites, singers and gatekeepers (vv. 43-45), and temple servants (vv. 46-60).
verseByVerse.theology: It is the same list as Ezra 2, copied a second time, and the repetition is the point: Nehemiah's people are the people God brought home. Where the numbers differ between the copies, the differences are reported below rather than hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: These were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried into exile. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his town. They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary: Twelve leaders; Ezra's copy names eleven. Twelve is the number of the tribes: this small company was all Israel in miniature. The Nehemiah and Mordecai in the list are other men of the same names, who came home ninety years before the governor telling this story.
verseByVerse.note: The list matches Ezra 2, with small differences in names and numbers.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Parosh, 2,172. The sons of Shephatiah, 372. The sons of Arah, 652. The sons of Pahath-moab, namely the sons of Jeshua and Joab, 2,818. The sons of Elam, 1,254. The sons of Zattu, 845. The sons of Zaccai, 760. The sons of Binnui, 648. The sons of Bebai, 628. The sons of Azgad, 2,322. The sons of Adonikam, 667. The sons of Bigvai, 2,067. The sons of Adin, 655. The sons of Ater, namely of Hezekiah, 98. The sons of Hashum, 328. The sons of Bezai, 324. The sons of Hariph, 112. The sons of Gibeon, 95.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the families, eighteen lines of names and numbers. Most of these people appear nowhere else in the Bible. They are here because they left Babylon, where most Jews stayed, for a ruined country and an uncertain welcome, on the strength of a promise.

A word on the numbers, since a careful reader will compare this chapter with Ezra 2 and find that many of them differ. The family of Adonikam is 666 in Ezra and 667 here; Azgad is 1,222 there and 2,322 here. Numbers are the easiest thing in any manuscript to miscopy, and these are two copies of one list made by hand. Some also think the two copies were brought up to date at different times. With the historic confessions, this commentary holds that Scripture as first given is without error; slips like these crept in as scribes copied long columns of figures, and the copies we have let us see them plainly. Nothing in the faith hangs on the size of the family of Azgad. What the list is for does not change: God brought these people home.

verseByVerse.quote: The men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188. The men of Anathoth, 128. The men of Beth-azmaveth, 42. The men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743. The men of Ramah and Geba, 621. The men of Michmas, 122. The men of Bethel and Ai, 123. The men of the other Nebo, 52. The sons of the other Elam, 1,254. The sons of Harim, 320. The sons of Jericho, 345. The sons of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 721. The sons of Senaah, 3,930.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From here the list runs by towns, and the towns have histories. Bethlehem (v. 26) is the town of David, of which Micah had said, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel (Mic 5:2). Some of those 188 may have been forebears of families still living there when Joseph went up to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem (Luke 2:4). The Ruler was born in a town that had been emptied and then resettled by people on this list.

Anathoth (v. 27) was Jeremiah's town. With the Babylonian army outside Jerusalem, he had bought a field there, on God's word, as a sign that fields would again be bought in this land (Jer 32:15). Here are 128 men of Anathoth, home again, on land a prophet had paid for in a siege.

Put Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah and Beeroth (v. 29) beside Gibeon (v. 25) and you have the four cities of the Gibeonites, the Canaanites who deceived Joshua and were spared (Josh 9:17). Their descendants went into exile with Judah and came home with Judah, and in chapter 3 the men of Gibeon built a stretch of the wall. Kiriath-jearim is also where the ark stayed for decades, until David brought it up (1 Sam 7:1-2; 2 Sam 6:2-3). The ark had once rested in a town of the outsiders.

Then Michmas, where Jonathan climbed the cliff (1 Sam 14); Bethel and Ai, Jacob's ladder and Israel's first defeat, in one line (v. 32); Jericho, whose men built beside the high priest (3:2); and Ono (v. 37), the plain where Sanballat tried to lure Nehemiah (6:2). There were Jewish families living there, which is perhaps why the invitation sounded reasonable.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, namely the house of Jeshua, 973. The sons of Immer, 1,052. The sons of Pashhur, 1,247. The sons of Harim, 1,017.
verseByVerse.commentary: Four priestly families, 4,289 men. Add them up and set them against the next verse: the Levites, who assisted the priests, number seventy-four. The priests had a great deal to come home to, and the Levites, whose work was the carrying and serving, had not come. When Ezra brought his own company, eighty years later, he had to send back specially for Levites because he found none (Ezra 8:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites: the sons of Jeshua, namely of Kadmiel of the sons of Hodevah, 74. The singers: the sons of Asaph, 148. The gatekeepers: the sons of Shallum, the sons of Ater, the sons of Talmon, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hatita, the sons of Shobai, 138. The temple servants: the sons of Ziha, the sons of Hasupha, the sons of Tabbaoth, the sons of Keros, the sons of Sia, the sons of Padon, the sons of Lebana, the sons of Hagaba, the sons of Shalmai, the sons of Hanan, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Gahar, the sons of Reaiah, the sons of Rezin, the sons of Nekoda, the sons of Gazzam, the sons of Uzza, the sons of Paseah, the sons of Besai, the sons of Meunim, the sons of Nephushesim, the sons of Bakbuk, the sons of Hakupha, the sons of Harhur, the sons of Bazlith, the sons of Mehida, the sons of Harsha, the sons of Barkos, the sons of Sisera, the sons of Temah, the sons of Neziah, the sons of Hatipha. The sons of Solomon's servants: the sons of Sotai, the sons of Sophereth, the sons of Perida, the sons of Jaala, the sons of Darkon, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Shephatiah, the sons of Hattil, the sons of Pochereth-hazzebaim, the sons of Amon. All the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants were 392.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singers are the descendants of Asaph, David's chief musician; ninety years after the return they are still singing his psalms, and Nehemiah has just appointed them again (v. 1).

Then the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants, 392 between them (v. 60), probably descended from foreigners given to the work of the temple long before (Ezra 8:20). Families who began as outsiders and servants are listed in the register of God's people, alongside the priests.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 61–73 — Until a Priest Should Arise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some could not prove their descent, and three priestly families were barred until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise (vv. 61-65). The total, the servants and animals (vv. 66-69), the gifts (vv. 70-72), and the seventh month (v. 73).
verseByVerse.theology: The register ends on an open question about who is a priest, and on a date. Ezra 3 opens with the same sentence, and in both books what follows is the people gathering in Jerusalem as one man.

verseByVerse.quote: The following were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not prove their fathers' houses nor their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: the sons of Delaiah, the sons of Tobiah, the sons of Nekoda, 642. Also, of the priests: the sons of Hobaiah, the sons of Hakkoz, the sons of Barzillai (who had taken a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name). These sought their registration among those enrolled in the genealogies, but it was not found there, so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them that they were not to partake of the most holy food until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the hard part of the list. Some came home but they could not prove their fathers' houses nor their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: 642 people of three families (vv. 61-62). They are not sent away. They are simply recorded as unproven.

And three families of priests searched for their names in the records and could not find them, and were barred from the most holy food until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise. The Urim and Thummim were the means by which the high priest had once received God's answer to a question. There was no one who could use them. So the question was left open, waiting for God.

The third of those families has a sad little story in its bracket. A priest had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite, who fed David in his flight from Absalom (2 Sam 19:31-32), and took the famous name of his wife's family; his descendants lost the name that made them priests. It is possible to gain a distinguished name and lose a birthright.

Remember Hakkoz. In chapter 3 Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, built two sections of the wall (3:4, 21), and Ezra calls him Meremoth the priest (Ezra 8:33). Somewhere in those eighty years the family that could not find its name was found. God had not forgotten them.

And one Priest did arise who could not have passed this test either. It is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests (Heb 7:14). He had no priestly genealogy to produce. He has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:16). Everyone who cannot prove his place before God can have it through him.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole assembly together was 42,360, besides their male and female servants, of whom there were 7,337. And they had 245 singers, male and female. Their horses were 736, their mules 245, their camels 435, and their donkeys 6,720.
verseByVerse.commentary: Do the arithmetic and something does not add up. The family and town figures in this chapter (vv. 8-62) total 31,089, and the stated total is 42,360, so 11,271 people are unaccounted for. Ezra's copy has the same total, and its figures come to 29,818. Perhaps the total counts people the family lists do not, such as members of other tribes or families not listed by name; perhaps the difference lies in the copying. The honest answer is that we do not know. The singers, too, are 245 here and 200 in Ezra. None of this is hidden, and none of it touches the point: tens of thousands came home, with their servants and their donkeys, because God had said they would.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the heads of fathers' houses gave to the work. The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 darics of gold, 50 basins, 30 priests' garments and 500 minas of silver. And some of the heads of fathers' houses gave into the treasury of the work 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver. And what the rest of the people gave was 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 priests' garments. So the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, some of the people, the temple servants, and all Israel, lived in their towns. And when the seventh month had come, the people of Israel were in their towns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The governor here is probably the governor of the first return, since this is still the old register, though some think Nehemiah's own gift is meant. Then the heads of families gave, and the rest of the people.

Ezra's copy gives round totals (Ezra 2:69), and Nehemiah's itemized gifts come close to them in silver and garments. And notice the rest of the people: the ordinary families gave as much gold as the heads of houses.

That last sentence is also the opening of Ezra 3 (Ezra 3:1). Ninety years earlier the list ended, the seventh month came, and the people gathered as one man to build an altar. Now the list ends, the seventh month comes, and the next verse says all the people gathered as one man (8:1). This time they ask for a book. The sacrifice first, then the Word: God had given them both, and the city was about to be filled with the second.
verseByVerse.note: A daric was a gold coin of about 1/4 ounce, a mina about 1¼ pounds (ESV notes).

7.theology:
A wall does not make a city; a people does. Nehemiah defines the people of the rebuilt city by the people God had brought home, and the list of ordinary families is itself a record of God's faithfulness to his promise to gather (1:9).

The register leaves open who is a priest, until a priest should arise who could answer for God. Christ is that Priest, though he had no priestly genealogy at all, being of Judah; he is priest by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:14-16).
7.examples:
A new wall round an empty city.

Hananiah was chosen because he feared God more than most.

188 men of Bethlehem and Netophah came home; the Ruler would be born in Bethlehem.

128 men of Anathoth came home to land a prophet had bought during the siege.

The figures add up to 31,089; the total says 42,360. The text does not hide it.

The family of Hakkoz, barred for want of a genealogy, later produced a priest who built two sections of the wall.
