8.overview: On the first day of the seventh month the whole people gather as one man at the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring the Book of the Law. He reads from dawn to midday; the people stand, answer Amen, Amen, and bow to the ground, while the Levites explain, so that the people understood the reading (vv. 1-8). They weep as they hear the law, but their leaders declare the day holy: go and feast, send portions to those who have nothing, for the joy of the LORD is your strength (vv. 9-12). On the second day the leaders study the law and find the command to live in booths, and the whole community does so as it had not since Joshua, with very great rejoicing, hearing the law read every day of the feast (vv. 13-18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the first day of the seventh month all the people gather in the square before the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring the Book of the Law (vv. 1-2). He reads from early morning until midday to men, women and all who could understand, and every ear is attentive (v. 3). He opens the book on a wooden platform, the people stand, and they answer his blessing with Amen, Amen and faces to the ground (vv. 4-6). The Levites read clearly and give the sense (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: The walls were finished to protect this: a people gathered round God's Word, wanting it, standing for it, and having it made plain.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people gathered as one man into the square before the Water Gate. And they told Ezra the scribe to bring the Book of the Law of Moses that the LORD had commanded Israel. So Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly, both men and women and all who could understand what they heard, on the first day of the seventh month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As one man. Ninety years before, when the first exiles had come home, the seventh month came and the people gathered as one man to build an altar (Ezra 3:1). Now the wall is up, the seventh month has come again (7:73), and they gather in the square by the Water Gate, below the temple. And the striking thing is who asks. It is not Nehemiah calling a meeting, or Ezra announcing a lecture. The people wanted to hear it.

Men and women, and every child old enough to follow: Moses had commanded this very scene, that they might hear and learn to fear the LORD your God (Deut 31:12). And the first day of the seventh month was a holy day already, a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets (Lev 23:24). The trumpets had called them together. The book told them why.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the seventh month was the Feast of Trumpets.

verseByVerse.quote: And he read from it facing the square before the Water Gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women and those who could understand. And the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From first light to noon: five or six hours, standing in an open square as the sun climbed, the length of a working day spent listening to Scripture. And they listened.

Put that beside Nehemiah's first prayer. In Susa he had asked God, let your ear be attentive (1:6). God had heard, and the wall was the proof. Now the direction is reversed, and the people's ears are attentive to God. That is what the whole building project was for.

How long could we listen, not to a sermon about Scripture, but to Scripture itself? These people had been without a clear reading of the law for most of their lives, and they were hungry for it. We have it in our own language beside the bed, and hunger is the thing we most often lack. It cannot be manufactured; it is asked for, from the Lord who still opens minds to the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform that they had made for the purpose. And beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah on his right hand, and Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam on his left hand. And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and as he opened it all the people stood. And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, "Amen, Amen," lifting up their hands. And they bowed their heads and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The platform is literally a tower: a raised wooden stand, built for the day, so that a crowd filling a city square could see and hear. Thirteen leaders stood with him, beside the reader, not in front of him.

The scroll was unrolled in front of them, and as it opened the whole square rose to its feet. Nobody had to tell them to. They stood because God was about to speak. Centuries later, in Nazareth, a man stood up to read, unrolled the scroll of Isaiah, and said, Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (Luke 4:16, 21).

Amen means it is true, let it be so. They said it twice, with their hands up, and then went down on their faces. Before a word of the law had been read, they had agreed with it and bowed to it. That is the posture in which Scripture is rightly heard.

And Ezra named him the great God, the title Nehemiah had prayed to in Susa (1:5) and shouted to the builders (4:14). The God great enough to turn a king and finish a wall was now great enough to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: Also Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, the Levites, helped the people to understand the Law, while the people remained in their places. They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirteen Levites move among the crowd as Ezra reads. The people stay where they are; the teachers come to them.

This one sentence describes what preaching is for. Three things. They read the text itself, the Law of God, not something about it. They read it clearly; the ESV's note offers "with interpretation" or "paragraph by paragraph", and many think it included putting the Hebrew into Aramaic, the everyday language most of these people had grown up with in exile. And they gave the sense: they explained it, so that the meaning got through. The test was not whether the teachers had been impressive. It was so that the people understood.

The greatest Teacher did exactly this. On the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself; and afterwards he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:27, 45). The Levites could explain the law. Only Christ could open the mind that hears it, and he still does.

Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and Hodiah will lead the people in confessing their sins in the next chapter (9:4-5). The men who explained the law lead the prayer it produced. Teaching that is understood turns into prayer.
verseByVerse.note: “Clearly” may mean “with interpretation” — perhaps translated into Aramaic for those who no longer spoke Hebrew.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — The Joy of the LORD Is Your Strength
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people weep as they hear the law. Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites tell them the day is holy to the LORD their God: go and feast, send portions to anyone who has nothing, and do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is their strength (vv. 9-11). They go home to make great rejoicing, because they had understood (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: A week after the wall was finished, Nehemiah tells them that their real fortress is the joy of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: And Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who taught the people said to all the people, "This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep." For all the people wept as they heard the words of the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They wept because they understood. They heard what God had commanded, and they knew their fathers had not done it, and neither had they: commands about the Sabbath, about marriage, about the poor, and they were standing in the ruins the curses had made. The law had done what it is for: through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom 3:20).

Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe stand side by side here, one of the few places they do (8:9; 12:26, 36). And their first word to a weeping crowd is not that they should weep more. It is this day is holy to the LORD your God. God had not called them together to grieve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, "Go your way. Eat the fat and drink sweet wine and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready, for this day is holy to our Lord. And do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go home and feast: the best cuts of meat, sweet wine, and portions for anyone who has nothing, so no one in the city is left out. It is the custom Esther records for Purim, gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor (Esth 9:22). God's holy days are feasts, and feasts are shared.

The word for strength is the word for a stronghold, a fortress: the LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? (Ps 27:1). They had spent fifty-two days building a wall with swords at their sides. Now Nehemiah tells them where their real fortress is. It is not the wall. It is the joy of the LORD.

Whose joy? The words can mean joy in the LORD, the gladness of people who know him; and they can mean the LORD's own joy, his delight over his people. Scripture gives us both. He will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing (Zeph 3:17). The people standing in that square, weeping over broken commands, were the people God was singing over. Their tears were right. But the fortress that would hold them was not how sorry they were. It was how glad he was to have them back.

That is still the order. Anyone who has seen his own sin clearly knows the weeping. The joy that holds a Christian up is not a feeling he generates; it is the Father's joy over a son come home (Luke 15:24), bought by the One who kept the law we have broken and for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (Heb 12:2).

verseByVerse.quote: So the Levites calmed all the people, saying, "Be quiet, for this day is holy; do not be grieved." And all the people went their way to eat and drink and to send portions and to make great rejoicing, because they had understood the words that were declared to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites go through the crowd as they had during the reading, now with a different message: hush, this is a holy day, stop grieving. The men who explained the law explained that it was a feast.

Because they had understood. The same understanding that made them weep in the morning made them rejoice in the afternoon. Nothing new had been read. What had changed was that they understood not only what God required but what kind of God had given it and called them to a feast in spite of all they had failed to do. Joy that does not come from understanding does not last. This did.

The two disciples on the Emmaus road knew the same thing: their hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures (Luke 24:32), and they went back to Jerusalem with great joy (Luke 24:52). Understood Scripture, opened by the Lord, ends in joy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the second day the leaders study the law and find the command to live in booths (vv. 13-15). The people build booths all over the city, as had not been done since Joshua, with very great rejoicing (vv. 16-17), and the law is read every day of the feast (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Booths remembered the wilderness, when God's people lived in tents and God lived among them in his. It was at this feast, on its last great day, that Jesus stood up in the temple and cried, If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37).

verseByVerse.quote: On the second day the heads of fathers' houses of all the people, with the priests and the Levites, came together to Ezra the scribe in order to study the words of the Law. And they found it written in the Law that the LORD had commanded by Moses that the people of Israel should dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month, and that they should proclaim it and publish it in all their towns and in Jerusalem, "Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees to make booths, as it is written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day the leaders are back. Having heard it once, they want to understand it better, so that they can lead their households in it. That is how you tell a real hearing of God's Word from an emotional one: the next day you want more of it.

The Feast of Booths began on the fifteenth of this month, only two weeks away (Lev 23:34), and the command came with the redemption it remembered: they were to live in booths that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt (Lev 23:43). So word went out to every town to bring branches.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people went out and brought them and made booths for themselves, each on his roof, and in their courts and in the courts of the house of God, and in the square at the Water Gate and in the square at the Gate of Ephraim. And all the assembly of those who had returned from the captivity made booths and lived in the booths, for from the days of Jeshua the son of Nun to that day the people of Israel had not done so. And there was very great rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Imagine the city that week: flat roofs covered with shelters of green branches, courtyards full of them, the temple courts, the squares by the gates. The empty city of 7:4 had filled with people living outdoors under leaves.

That sentence needs care, because the feast itself had been kept. Solomon kept it (2 Chr 8:13), and the first returnees kept it ninety years before: they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written (Ezra 3:4). What had not happened since Joshua was this: the whole assembly, every household, actually living in booths for the week, as the law commanded. Many had kept the sacrifices of the feast. Not since the conquest had the people as a whole done it in the way God had described.

Look too at the name in that sentence. Jeshua is the same name as Joshua, and in Greek it is Jesus. The first Joshua brought the people into the land, but he did not bring them into God's final rest: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on (Heb 4:8). These returned exiles in their booths were still pilgrims, as their fathers had been in the wilderness. Their rest was still to come, with a greater Jeshua.

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read from the Book of the Law of God. They kept the feast seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the rule.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every day of the feast the book was read, Moses' command kept to the letter: you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing (Deut 31:11). A week of living in the open, eating together and hearing God's Word, and then the great closing assembly.

Nearly five centuries later, on the last day of this same feast, the Word himself stood in the temple courts and offered rivers of living water to anyone who thirsts (John 7:37-38). The people in their booths remembered that God had once lived among them in a tent. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The feast of booths was waiting for him.

8.theology:
The wall was built to protect this: a people gathered round the Word of God, read and made plain. The Word first shows them their sin, and they weep; then it declares the day holy and sends them to feast. Law and gospel, grief and joy, in the right order.

The joy of the LORD is your strength: their stronghold was not the wall but the joy of a God who rejoices over his people (Zeph 3:17). Christ opens the Scriptures so that hearts burn (Luke 24:32), endured the cross for the joy set before him (Heb 12:2), and stood up on the last day of this very feast to offer living water to anyone who thirsts (John 7:37-38).
8.examples:
The people asked for the book.

They listened from first light to noon.

When the scroll opened, the whole square stood up.

They said Amen, Amen before the reading began.

The Levites read clearly and gave the sense, so that people understood.

They wept because they understood; they rejoiced because they understood.

A week after the wall, Nehemiah said their fortress was the joy of the LORD.

The city's roofs were covered with booths of branches.

9.title: The God Who Never Gave Up
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now on the twenty-fourth day of this month the people of Israel were assembled with fasting and in sackcloth, and with earth on their heads.<sup>2</sup>And the Israelites separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers.<sup>3</sup>And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day; for another quarter of it they made confession and worshiped the LORD their God.<sup>4</sup>On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani; and they cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God.<sup>5</sup>Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.<sup>6</sup>"You are the LORD, you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them; and the host of heaven worships you.<sup>7</sup>You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham.<sup>8</sup>You found his heart faithful before you, and made with him the covenant to give to his offspring the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite. And you have kept your promise, for you are righteous.<sup>9</sup>"And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea,<sup>10</sup>and performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants and all the people of his land, for you knew that they acted arrogantly against our fathers. And you made a name for yourself, as it is to this day.<sup>11</sup>And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters.<sup>12</sup>By a pillar of cloud you led them in the day, and by a pillar of fire in the night to light for them the way in which they should go.<sup>13</sup>You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven and gave them right rules and true laws, good statutes and commandments,<sup>14</sup>and you made known to them your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments and statutes and a law by Moses your servant.<sup>15</sup>You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and you told them to go in to possess the land that you had sworn to give them.<sup>16</sup>"But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments.<sup>17</sup>They refused to obey and were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them, but they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and did not forsake them.<sup>18</sup>Even when they had made for themselves a golden calf and said, 'This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,' and had committed great blasphemies,<sup>19</sup>you in your great mercies did not forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud to lead them in the way did not depart from them by day, nor the pillar of fire by night to light for them the way by which they should go.<sup>20</sup>You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your manna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst.<sup>21</sup>Forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell.<sup>22</sup>"And you gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted to them every corner. So they took possession of the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan.<sup>23</sup>You multiplied their children as the stars of heaven, and you brought them into the land that you had told their fathers to enter and possess.<sup>24</sup>So the descendants went in and possessed the land, and you subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hand, with their kings and the peoples of the land, that they might do with them as they would.<sup>25</sup>And they captured fortified cities and a rich land, and took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already hewn, vineyards, olive orchards and fruit trees in abundance. So they ate and were filled and became fat and delighted themselves in your great goodness.<sup>26</sup>"Nevertheless, they were disobedient and rebelled against you and cast your law behind their back and killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies.<sup>27</sup>Therefore you gave them into the hand of their enemies, who made them suffer. And in the time of their suffering they cried out to you and you heard them from heaven, and according to your great mercies you gave them saviors who saved them from the hand of their enemies.<sup>28</sup>But after they had rest they did evil again before you, and you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, so that they had dominion over them. Yet when they turned and cried to you, you heard from heaven, and many times you delivered them according to your mercies.<sup>29</sup>And you warned them in order to turn them back to your law. Yet they acted presumptuously and did not obey your commandments, but sinned against your rules, which if a person does them, he shall live by them, and they turned a stubborn shoulder and stiffened their neck and would not obey.<sup>30</sup>Many years you bore with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets. Yet they would not give ear. Therefore you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands.<sup>31</sup>Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God.<sup>32</sup>"Now, therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship seem little to you that has come upon us, upon our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until this day.<sup>33</sup>Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully and we have acted wickedly.<sup>34</sup>Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept your law or paid attention to your commandments and your warnings that you gave them.<sup>35</sup>Even in their own kingdom, and amid your great goodness that you gave them, and in the large and rich land that you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their wicked works.<sup>36</sup>Behold, we are slaves this day; in the land that you gave to our fathers to enjoy its fruit and its good gifts, behold, we are slaves.<sup>37</sup>And its rich yield goes to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress.<sup>38</sup>"Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing; on the sealed document are the names of our princes, our Levites, and our priests.
9.overview: Two days after Booths the people gather in fasting and sackcloth, read the law for a quarter of the day and confess for another (vv. 1-3). The Levites call them to stand and bless God (vv. 4-5), and the great prayer tells Israel's history as the history of God: the only Creator (v. 6); the God who chose Abraham and kept his promise (vv. 7-8); the Exodus, Sinai, manna and water (vv. 9-15). Then Israel's rebellion, answered each time by a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, from the calf to the prophets they killed, until you did not make an end of them or forsake them (vv. 16-31). It closes on the present: God has been righteous in all of it, and they are slaves in their own land (vv. 32-37). So they make a firm covenant in writing (v. 38).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Stand Up and Bless the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people assemble in fasting and sackcloth and confess their sins and their fathers' (vv. 1-2). They read the law and confess for a quarter of the day each (v. 3), and the Levites call them to stand and bless the LORD (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The fasting came after the feasting, not before. They had been told first that the joy of the LORD was their strength (8:10), and only then did they sit in sackcloth.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the twenty-fourth day of this month the people of Israel were assembled with fasting and in sackcloth, and with earth on their heads. And the Israelites separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day; for another quarter of it they made confession and worshiped the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two days after the last day of Booths. Three weeks earlier they had wept at the reading of the law and been told to stop, because it was a feast day (8:9-11). Now the feast is over, and the grief that was postponed is given its day.

People who already know God's delight in them can look at their sin without flinching and without despair. Confession that begins from terror usually stops short. Confession that begins from joy can go all the way down.

The separation was not a rejection of any foreigner who had joined himself to the LORD (the Passover of Ezra 6:21 welcomed such), but a day on which Israel stood before God as Israel and owned its own history: not the present alone, but the iniquities of their fathers.

Three hours of Scripture, then three hours of confession and worship. The reading came first, because a people cannot confess sins it has not been shown. The Word told them what to confess, and the worship told them to whom.

verseByVerse.quote: On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani; and they cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God. Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Several of these Levites had moved through the crowd three weeks before, helping the people understand the law (8:7). The teachers now lead the prayer. Understanding has become confession.

They are in sackcloth, about to confess centuries of failure, and the first word is bless. The confession will be addressed to a God whose name is higher than any praise they can give, and that is what makes confession safe. You can tell the whole truth about yourself to a God like that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — You Are the LORD, You Alone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer begins with God alone, maker of heaven and earth and the seas and preserver of them all (v. 6), who chose Abram and made covenant with him, and kept his promise, for he is righteous (vv. 7-8). He saw Israel's affliction in Egypt, divided the sea, led them by cloud and fire (vv. 9-12), came down on Sinai and gave them good laws and his holy Sabbath (vv. 13-14), and fed them with bread from heaven and water from the rock (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Every verb in this part of the prayer has God for its subject. The history of Israel is told as the history of what God did.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the LORD, you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them; and the host of heaven worships you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer does not begin with Israel's trouble but with the universe. Before a word about Persian taxes or broken covenants, they say who God is: the only one, maker of the highest heaven and the deepest sea, keeping every one of them in being, and worshipped by the angels.

You alone was the confession their fathers had failed to make; it was the other gods that had sent them into exile. And it matters for everything that follows. If God is one of many, Israel's story is a contest between powers. If he alone made and holds all things, there has never been a moment in their history that was out of his hands, including the worst ones. The New Testament says who that Maker is: by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth ... all things were created through him and for him (Col 1:16).

verseByVerse.quote: You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham. You found his heart faithful before you, and made with him the covenant to give to his offspring the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite. And you have kept your promise, for you are righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the whole creation to one man. God chose him, brought him out, and renamed him; every verb is God's. And Ur of the Chaldeans is in Babylonia: the people praying had been brought out of the same country as their father Abraham.

You are righteous. Hold on to that phrase. Here it means that God kept his word: he promised the land and he gave it. In verse 33 it will come back — you have been righteous in all that has come upon us — and there it means that the exile was deserved. The prayer is bracketed by God's righteousness, once in the keeping of a promise and once in the carrying out of a sentence. He is the same God in both, and they trust him in both.

And look at the two words the verse puts together, faithful and righteous. Faithful is from the same Hebrew root as believed in the sentence the whole Bible turns on: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness (Gen 15:6). God found in Abraham a heart that believed him, and counted it righteousness; and God himself turned out to be the righteous one, keeping every word. Paul builds the gospel on that verse (Rom 4:3). Abraham's faith was never the ground of the promise. God's righteousness was.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea, and performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants and all the people of his land, for you knew that they acted arrogantly against our fathers. And you made a name for yourself, as it is to this day. And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You saw ... and heard. The prayer remembers a God who noticed. And the Exodus was not only a rescue; it was God making a name for himself, still his name all those centuries later.

Mark that charge. They acted arrogantly is said of Egypt, and in verse 16 the same Hebrew verb is used of Israel: they and our fathers acted presumptuously, and again in verse 29. The people God rescued from the arrogant became arrogant toward him. The prayer does not spare them the comparison. They had treated God the way Pharaoh had treated them.

The praying people knew what it was to be pursued by stronger nations. They remember the day God dropped the pursuers into the sea like a stone and the slaves walked through on dry ground.

verseByVerse.quote: By a pillar of cloud you led them in the day, and by a pillar of fire in the night to light for them the way in which they should go. You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven and gave them right rules and true laws, good statutes and commandments, and you made known to them your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments and statutes and a law by Moses your servant. You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and you told them to go in to possess the land that you had sworn to give them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you made known to them your holy Sabbath. Of all the commandments, the Sabbath is the one named. It was a gift: a day of rest given to people who had been slaves and had never had one. It will matter again when Nehemiah finds the gates open for trade on that day (13:15-22).

Both the bread and the water Jesus claimed for himself: My Father gives you the true bread from heaven ... I am the bread of life (John 6:32, 35). And Paul says of the rock: the Rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). The God who fed them in the desert was already giving them, in shadow, his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–31 — You Did Not Forsake Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Their fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck, even choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt, but God, ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, did not forsake them (vv. 16-17): not after the golden calf (vv. 18-21); not through the conquest, when they grew fat on houses they had not built (vv. 22-25); not when they killed the prophets and he gave them into their enemies' hands and then sent saviors (vv. 26-28); not when they turned a stubborn shoulder for many years (vv. 29-30). In his great mercies he did not make an end of them (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Three times the prayer says God did not forsake them (vv. 17, 19, 31). Once, you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies (v. 28). God gave them up for a time; he never gave them up for good.

verseByVerse.quote: "But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments. They refused to obey and were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them, but they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and did not forsake them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the other side. Stiffened their neck, twice: the ox that will not bend to the yoke, as the nobles of Tekoa would not (3:5). And the worst of it: a leader chosen to go back to Egypt (Num 14:4). A people freed from slavery and fed daily from heaven chose the brickworks rather than trust God for the land. Keep that in mind until verse 36, where the people praying say they are slaves this day. Their fathers had asked to be slaves, and had been given what they asked for.

This is the name God proclaimed to Moses on the mountain: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). And he proclaimed it immediately after the golden calf, the worst sin in their history. God did not reveal his mercy to people who had deserved it, but to people who had just proved they did not. A God ready to forgive (v. 17) is, in Hebrew, a God of forgivenesses, plural: forgiveness, and more of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Even when they had made for themselves a golden calf and said, 'This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,' and had committed great blasphemies, you in your great mercies did not forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud to lead them in the way did not depart from them by day, nor the pillar of fire by night to light for them the way by which they should go. You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your manna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst. Forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They credited a metal calf with the Exodus. And the very next thing the prayer records is that the pillar of cloud did not depart. The morning after the calf, the cloud was still there, described in almost the words of verse 12: nothing about God's leading had changed, though everything about their deserving had.

Moses had said the same of the sandals and the feet (Deut 8:4). A single pair of sandals, walked in for forty years and never worn through: that is the care of God for people in the middle of their rebellion. And first in the list is not food but your good Spirit to instruct them. God did not only feed rebels; he went on teaching them. The same Spirit is promised to believers now, to teach you all things (John 14:26).

Many readers know what it is to have wandered in some wilderness of their own making and to look back and see that God fed them the whole way. Their sandals did not wear out either. That is not a reason to presume on him. It is a reason to come home.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted to them every corner. So they took possession of the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan. You multiplied their children as the stars of heaven, and you brought them into the land that you had told their fathers to enter and possess. So the descendants went in and possessed the land, and you subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hand, with their kings and the peoples of the land, that they might do with them as they would. And they captured fortified cities and a rich land, and took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already hewn, vineyards, olive orchards and fruit trees in abundance. So they ate and were filled and became fat and delighted themselves in your great goodness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the land: kingdoms given, children multiplied as the stars of heaven, the Canaanites handed over (vv. 22-24). The stars go back to the night God told Abraham, So shall your offspring be (Gen 15:5). Verse 8 said he kept his promise; verse 23 shows it kept, in houses full of good things, cisterns, vineyards and orchards.

That is almost word for word what Moses had promised, and warned: houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant, and when you eat and are full, then take care lest you forget the LORD (Deut 6:11-12).

Delighted themselves in your great goodness: there is nothing wrong in that; it is what the gifts were for. But Moses had also sung what would happen next: Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked (Deut 32:15). The danger of blessing is that we come to love the house and forget who filled it. A test we can run on ourselves: when life is full, do we pray more, or less?

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, they were disobedient and rebelled against you and cast your law behind their back and killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies. Therefore you gave them into the hand of their enemies, who made them suffer. And in the time of their suffering they cried out to you and you heard them from heaven, and according to your great mercies you gave them saviors who saved them from the hand of their enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cast your law behind their back: not lost, not forgotten, but thrown over the shoulder so that they would not have to look at it. And killed your prophets: Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court for delivering God's message (2 Chr 24:20-21). Jesus wept over the same city for the same reason: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! (Luke 13:34). And then they killed him too.

That is the book of Judges in one sentence (Judg 3:9): one savior after another, each for a generation. They were waiting, without knowing it, for the announcement to the shepherds: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord (Luke 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: But after they had rest they did evil again before you, and you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, so that they had dominion over them. Yet when they turned and cried to you, you heard from heaven, and many times you delivered them according to your mercies. And you warned them in order to turn them back to your law. Yet they acted presumptuously and did not obey your commandments, but sinned against your rules, which if a person does them, he shall live by them, and they turned a stubborn shoulder and stiffened their neck and would not obey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not in hardship but in rest: it was the good years that undid them. And the word abandoned is honest. God did give them up to their enemies, for a time; what he never did was give them up for good. Many times you delivered them. Mercy that could be counted would have run out long before.

Which if a person does them, he shall live by them is Leviticus 18:5, the law's own promise: do this and live. They did not do it, and neither has anyone else. Paul quotes the same verse and then says what God did about it: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:12-13). The one Man who did them, and could have lived by them, died under the curse that belonged to those who did not.

verseByVerse.quote: Many years you bore with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets. Yet they would not give ear. Therefore you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands. Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many years: the prophets spoke for centuries, from Elijah to Jeremiah. A stubborn shoulder (v. 29) is an ox shrugging off the yoke, and Zechariah had used the same words of their fathers (Zech 7:11). He had also said whose voice they were refusing: the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets (Zech 7:12). The prophets' words were the Spirit's words. They were refusing God, not men. And so God gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands: the exile.

That nevertheless is the hinge of the whole history. The exile was deserved, and it was not the end. They were standing in Jerusalem saying so. Ezra had prayed the same: for we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery (Ezra 9:9).

And the reason God could promise never to forsake people who had forsaken him for centuries is that one day he would forsake someone else in their place. At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice ... My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34). He was abandoned so that his people would hear, and keep hearing, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb 13:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–38 — Behold, We Are Slaves This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer asks the great and awesome God not to think their hardship small (v. 32), and owns that he has been righteous in all of it (v. 33). They would not serve him in their own land (vv. 34-35), and now they are slaves in it (vv. 36-37). So they make a firm covenant in writing (v. 38).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer asks for one thing, that God would not think their hardship small, and it asks it while agreeing that every blow was deserved. It is the confession of people who know their only hope is the character of the God they have wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship seem little to you that has come upon us, upon our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until this day. Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully and we have acted wickedly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The history has reached the present, and the prayer turns to God with the words of Moses (Deut 10:17) and of Nehemiah's own first prayer (1:5). The one request in the entire prayer is modest: do not let our hardship look small to you. Since the time of the kings of Assyria: three centuries of invasion, deportation and subjection. Look at it, Lord. Do not treat it as nothing.

And in the same breath: it was all just. That is the heart of true confession. They ask God to see their suffering, and they agree with every stroke of it. No excuses, no blaming the kings of Assyria. The man who can pray verse 33 without an exception has been brought to the place where mercy can reach him.

verseByVerse.quote: Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept your law or paid attention to your commandments and your warnings that you gave them. Even in their own kingdom, and amid your great goodness that you gave them, and in the large and rich land that you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their wicked works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every rank is named; nobody is left outside the confession, with one exception. In verse 32 the hardship fell on our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers. In verse 34 the ones who did not keep the law are kings, princes, priests and fathers. The prophets have dropped out of the list. They suffered with the nation, went into exile with it (Jeremiah to Egypt, Ezekiel and Daniel to Babylon), and were not the cause of it. The innocent went down with the guilty. One Prophet went further, and suffered not only with the guilty but for them.

Their own kingdom: they had had a king of their own, a land of their own, and every good thing in it, and they did not serve you. Hold that thought. It is about to come back.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, we are slaves this day; in the land that you gave to our fathers to enjoy its fruit and its good gifts, behold, we are slaves. And its rich yield goes to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Slaves and serve come from the same Hebrew root. They would not serve God in their own kingdom (v. 35), and so they are slaves in their own land. God had said exactly this to Rehoboam's generation: they shall be servants to him, that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries (2 Chr 12:8). Every people serves someone. Refuse the service of God and you do not become free; you learn the service of the kingdoms. And the fathers who had once asked for a leader to take them back to slavery (v. 17) had got their wish.

The Persian king who sent Nehemiah had been generous to him, but the harvest of Judah still went east in tribute, and the empire could conscript their bodies and their animals as it pleased. Whom you have set over us: even the empire is God's doing. We are in great distress. The prayer ends there.

There is only one way out of that kind of slavery, and it is not a better master in Persia. If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:36).

verseByVerse.quote: "Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing; on the sealed document are the names of our princes, our Levites, and our priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because of all this: the whole history, the mercy and the rebellion, the slavery they are in. They answer not with a feeling but with a document, written, sealed and signed, so that there can be no quiet forgetting later. The next chapter is the list of those who signed and what they promised.

It is right to bind oneself to God in this way, and chapter 13 will show how quickly the promises of chapter 10 were broken. A covenant with our names on it cannot save us. What saves is the covenant with God's name on it, the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20), sealed by the one party who has never failed to keep his word, and giving the Spirit who causes his people to walk in his ways (Ezek 36:27).

9.theology:
The whole history is told with God as its subject. God is righteous in keeping his promise (v. 8) and righteous in the judgment (v. 33), and between those two verses his people rebel again and again and he does not forsake them. Mercy that could be counted would have run out.

The prayer lives on shadows that Christ fills: the bread from heaven and the rock (John 6:35; 1 Cor 10:4), the saviors of the judges (Luke 2:11), the prophets Jerusalem killed (Luke 13:34), the law that promises life to the one who does it (Lev 18:5), which he did and whose curse he bore (Gal 3:12-13). God could promise never to forsake a people who had forsaken him because he would forsake his Son in their place (Mark 15:34; Heb 13:5).
9.examples:
The fast came after the feast.

They read Scripture for three hours before they confessed for three.

In sackcloth, the first word was bless.

After the golden calf, the cloud was still there.

Forty years in the same sandals.

Their fathers asked for a leader back to slavery; the children say we are slaves this day.

They would not serve God, so they served Persia.

The one request: do not let our hardship seem small to you.

10.overview: The sealed covenant of 9:38 bears eighty-four names: Nehemiah the governor first, then priests, Levites and chiefs of the people, most of them family names of the first return (vv. 1-27). The rest of the people, with their wives and children and every convert who had separated himself to the Law of God, join them under a curse and an oath (vv. 28-29). The terms are specific: no marriages with the peoples of the land (v. 30); no buying on the Sabbath, the seventh year kept and debts released (v. 31); a yearly temple tax, wood for the altar, firstfruits and tithes (vv. 32-39). It ends: We will not neglect the house of our God (v. 39), a promise chapter 13 will find broken.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — On the Seals Are the Names
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the seals are the names of Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, Zedekiah (v. 1), then twenty-one priests (vv. 2-8), seventeen Levites (vv. 9-13), and forty-four chiefs of the people (vv. 14-27) — eighty-four names on the sealed document of 9:38.
verseByVerse.theology: They put their names to it, so that it could not be quietly forgotten later. The same names turn up in the next chapters, some keeping the promise and some breaking it.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the seals are the names of Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, Zedekiah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the signature page of the sealed document (9:38). A seal pressed into clay or wax was a man's signature in that world: this is mine, and I stand behind it.

The first name is the governor's. Nehemiah did not ask the people to bind themselves to anything he had not bound himself to first, as when he said let us abandon the interest (5:10). Zedekiah, next to him, was perhaps his secretary.

verseByVerse.quote: Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah, Pashhur, Amariah, Malchijah, Hattush, Shebaniah, Malluch, Harim, Meremoth, Obadiah, Daniel, Ginnethon, Baruch, Meshullam, Abijah, Mijamin, Maaziah, Bilgai, Shemaiah; these are the priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-one priests, most of them the names of priestly houses rather than individuals; many reappear in 12:1-21. A family signs through its head.

Two names stand out. Meremoth (v. 5) recalls the priest of the family of Hakkoz who built two sections of the wall (3:4, 21), from a family once barred for want of a genealogy (7:63-64). And Abijah (v. 7) will be heard of again. When David divided the priests, the lots fell the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah (1 Chr 24:10). More than four centuries after Nehemiah, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah (Luke 1:5), and while he served in the temple an angel told him he would have a son who would prepare the way for the Lord. The name on this seal is the division of John the Baptist's father.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Levites: Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel; and their brothers, Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan, Mica, Rehob, Hashabiah, Zaccur, Sherebiah, Shebaniah, Hodiah, Bani, Beninu.
verseByVerse.commentary: Seventeen Levites, several of them the men who explained the law at the Water Gate (8:7) and led the confession from the stairs (9:4-5). They taught it, they prayed it, and now they sign it, putting their own names under the obligations they had been explaining to everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: The chiefs of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani, Bunni, Azgad, Bebai, Adonijah, Bigvai, Adin, Ater, Hezekiah, Azzur, Hodiah, Hashum, Bezai, Hariph, Anathoth, Nebai, Magpiash, Meshullam, Hezir, Meshezabel, Zadok, Jaddua, Pelatiah, Hanan, Anaiah, Hoshea, Hananiah, Hasshub, Hallohesh, Pilha, Shobek, Rehum, Hashabnah, Maaseiah, Ahiah, Hanan, Anan, Malluch, Harim, Baanah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty-four chiefs of the people, and read against the register in chapter 7 most are old friends: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Azgad, Bebai and the rest, even Anathoth, which is a town. The children of the first return were renewing their fathers' covenant.

And a few names from the wall. Hallohesh (v. 24) is the family of Shallum, who built with his daughters (3:12). There is a Meshullam here too (v. 20), a common name, and the reader remembers another Meshullam who built two sections and then married his daughter to Tobiah's son (6:18). Names on a covenant are only as good as the hearts behind them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–31 — To Walk in God's Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the people, with all who have separated themselves to the Law of God, join under a curse and an oath (vv. 28-29). No marriages with the peoples of the land (v. 30); no buying on the Sabbath; the seventh year and the release of debts (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant addresses the three places where the community had actually been failing: its marriages, its Sabbaths and its debts. It is specific because their disobedience had been specific.

verseByVerse.quote: "The rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants, and all who have separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the Law of God, their wives, their sons, their daughters, all who have knowledge and understanding, join with their brothers, their nobles, and enter into a curse and an oath to walk in God's Law that was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord and his rules and his statutes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who could understand, as at the reading (8:2), wives and daughters included. And belonging is defined by a separation to the Law of God: toward something. A foreigner who turned from his gods to the LORD was inside this sentence, as such people had been at the Passover (Ezra 6:21). The line runs round a way of worship, not round a bloodline.

And they join with their brothers, their nobles: the same people who had raised a great outcry against the nobles holding their fields and daughters (5:1-5). The debts had been returned, and the brothers were brothers again. Reconciliation came before the covenant, not after it.

A curse and an oath: they swore, and called down on themselves the curses of the law if they broke it. That is a serious thing to do, and they meant it. Chapter 13 will show how much it was worth in practice. It is also the reason we need a better covenant than one we can sign ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land or take their daughters for our sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is Deuteronomy 7:3, and the law gave its reason in the next verse: they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut 7:4). The concern is the worship of the home, not the blood of the partner, which is why the proselyte is included in verse 28. Nehemiah will find the promise broken by the time he comes back from Persia, with children who could not speak the language of Judah (13:23-24).

A Christian reader will want to know how this applies now, and the New Testament answers both halves plainly. To the unmarried: marry only in the Lord (1 Cor 7:39). To the believer who is already married to an unbeliever: he should not divorce her, and she should not divorce him, for the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife (1 Cor 7:12-14). The promise of this verse is about marriages not yet made. It gives no one a warrant to leave a marriage that already exists.

verseByVerse.quote: And if the peoples of the land bring in goods or any grain on the Sabbath day to sell, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day. And we will forgo the crops of the seventh year and the exaction of every debt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sabbath law forbade Israel to work; it did not stop foreign traders from setting up stalls. The covenant closes the gap: if we cannot sell, we will not buy either. It is exactly this gap that Nehemiah finds wide open in 13:15-16.

Every seventh year the land was to lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat (Exod 23:11), and debts between Israelites were to be released (Deut 15:2). That is chapter 5 written into law. The fathers who had sold their daughters for debt (5:5) now have it sealed by the nobles that debts will not grind a family down for ever.

A test for a Christian's week: is there anything in the way we buy, sell and lend that says we belong to a God who gives rest and forgives debts? The Sabbath and the seventh year were God's people saying with their calendars and their account books that they trusted him to provide.

Does the Sabbath bind Christians today? It was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exod 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col 2:16–17). This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Heb 4:9–10), so no day binds the conscience (Rom 14:5); Christians gladly keep the Lord’s Day for worship and rest as a gift. Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. Faithful believers differ here and can differ as brothers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–39 — We Will Not Neglect the House of Our God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A yearly temple tax (vv. 32-33), wood for the altar by lot (v. 34), and firstfruits, firstborn and tithes for the priests and Levites (vv. 35-39): they will not neglect the house of their God.
verseByVerse.theology: In the prayer of chapter 9 they confessed that God did not forsake them. Now they promise not to neglect his house. In chapter 13 Nehemiah will come back and ask, Why is the house of God forsaken? (13:11).

verseByVerse.quote: "We also take on ourselves the obligation to give yearly a third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God: for the showbread, the regular grain offering, the regular burnt offering, the Sabbaths, the new moons, the appointed feasts, the holy things, and the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law had set a half shekel for each man, rich and poor alike, to make atonement for your lives (Exod 30:15). The community, poor and in debt, pledges a third, every year. By Jesus' day the tax was back at the half shekel, and Jesus asked whether kings tax their own sons: Then the sons are free. The Son owed nothing to his Father's house, and paid it anyway, with a coin from a fish's mouth: give it to them for me and for yourself (Matt 17:26-27). One coin, for the Son and for the disciple together.

The tax paid, year after year, for the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel. The offerings never stopped because the sins never stopped. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down (Heb 10:11-12). The standing order for atonement was cancelled when the account was paid in full.
verseByVerse.note: A third of a shekel each year for the temple; the law had set a half shekel (Exod 30:13), and by Jesus’ day the tax was a half shekel again.

verseByVerse.quote: We, the priests, the Levites, and the people, have likewise cast lots for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God, according to our fathers' houses, at times appointed, year by year, to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No law in the Pentateuch sets up a rota for firewood. What is written is that the fire on the altar shall not go out (Lev 6:12), and if it must never go out, somebody must bring the wood. This is obedience taking a command seriously enough to work out the practical cost.

It is also nearly the last thing Nehemiah mentions in his whole book: and I provided for the wood offering at appointed times, and for the firstfruits (13:31). Among the final entries in a great man's record is the firewood.

verseByVerse.quote: We obligate ourselves to bring the firstfruits of our ground and the firstfruits of all fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of the LORD; also to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God, the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle, as it is written in the Law, and the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks; and to bring the first of our dough, and our contributions, the fruit of every tree, the wine and the oil, to the priests, to the chambers of the house of our God; and to bring to the Levites the tithes from our ground, for it is the Levites who collect the tithes in all our towns where we labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the firsts: firstfruits, firstborn, the first of the dough, each a law of Moses (Exod 23:19; 13:13; Num 15:20). The first of everything went to God, before the family ate or sold any of it. The firstborn sons were redeemed with a price, a reminder that every family owed its eldest to the God who spared them on the night of the Passover.

The tithes go to the Levites, who had no land of their own and lived on what God's people gave. If the tithes stopped, the Levites went back to the fields and the temple service stopped with them. That is exactly what Nehemiah will find: the Levites and the singers, who did the work, had fled each to his field (13:10).

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Gal 6:6; 1 Cor 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest, the son of Aaron, shall be with the Levites when the Levites receive the tithes. And the Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes to the house of our God, to the chambers of the storehouse. For the people of Israel and the sons of Levi shall bring the contribution of grain, wine, and oil to the chambers, where the vessels of the sanctuary are, as well as the priests who minister, and the gatekeepers and the singers. We will not neglect the house of our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A priest is present at every collection, so that the counting is witnessed, and the Levites give a tenth of what they receive (Num 18:26). Nobody is exempt from giving, not even the people who live on the gifts.

Notice how often the chambers are mentioned (vv. 37-39): the temple storerooms for the Levites' grain, wine and oil. Remember them. In chapter 13 Nehemiah finds that Eliashib the priest has emptied one and moved Tobiah the Ammonite into it, furniture and all (13:4-5).

Neglect is the Hebrew word translated forsake in the great prayer, which had confessed, you ... did not forsake them (9:19). God had not forsaken them through centuries of rebellion; they answer, then we will not neglect your house. Years later Nehemiah will ask, Why is the house of God forsaken? (13:11).

That is not a reason to despise their promise. It was right and good. It is a reason to see why a covenant signed by us, however sincerely, is not enough. The new covenant is the one in which God makes the promises and keeps both sides: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33), and he gives his Spirit to cause his people to walk in his ways (Ezek 36:27). Where we break what we have signed, Christ kept his Father's will perfectly in our place, and the house of God is safe in the hands of the Son, of whom it was written, Zeal for your house will consume me (John 2:17).

10.theology:
After hearing the law and confessing their history, the people bind themselves in writing to specific obedience in the very places they had failed: marriage, Sabbath, debt, and the support of God's house. It is right that God's people make such commitments, and chapter 13 shows why such commitments cannot save them.

The yearly tax paid for sin offerings that never ended until Christ offered one sacrifice for all time (Heb 10:11-12). The Son who owed no tax to his Father's house paid it for himself and his disciple (Matt 17:26-27), and the new covenant is the one God keeps from both sides (Jer 31:33).
10.examples:
The governor signed first.

The priestly house of Abijah set its seal here; John the Baptist's father was of that division.

The Levites who taught the law and led the confession signed it too.

The debt reform of chapter 5 was written into the covenant.

They worked out a firewood rota because the fire on the altar must never go out.

They ended with a promise: We will not neglect the house of our God.

11.title: Who Will Live in the Holy City?
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the leaders of the people lived in Jerusalem. And the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in Jerusalem the holy city, while nine out of ten remained in the other towns.<sup>2</sup>And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>These are the chiefs of the province who lived in Jerusalem; but in the towns of Judah everyone lived on his property in their towns: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the descendants of Solomon's servants.<sup>4</sup>And in Jerusalem lived certain of the sons of Judah and of the sons of Benjamin. Of the sons of Judah: Athaiah the son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, of the sons of Perez;<sup>5</sup>and Maaseiah the son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite.<sup>6</sup>All the sons of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were 468 valiant men.<sup>7</sup>And these are the sons of Benjamin: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah,<sup>8</sup>and his brothers, men of valor, 928.<sup>9</sup>Joel the son of Zichri was their overseer; and Judah the son of Hassenuah was second over the city.<sup>10</sup>Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin,<sup>11</sup>Seraiah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, ruler of the house of God,<sup>12</sup>and their brothers who did the work of the house, 822; and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah,<sup>13</sup>and his brothers, heads of fathers' houses, 242; and Amashsai, the son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer,<sup>14</sup>and their brothers, mighty men of valor, 128; their overseer was Zabdiel the son of Haggedolim.<sup>15</sup>And of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni;<sup>16</sup>and Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chiefs of the Levites, who were over the outside work of the house of God;<sup>17</sup>and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, who was the leader of the praise, who gave thanks, and Bakbukiah, the second among his brothers; and Abda the son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun.<sup>18</sup>All the Levites in the holy city were 284.<sup>19</sup>The gatekeepers, Akkub, Talmon and their brothers, who kept watch at the gates, were 172.<sup>20</sup>And the rest of Israel, and of the priests and the Levites, were in all the towns of Judah, every one in his inheritance.<sup>21</sup>But the temple servants lived on Ophel; and Ziha and Gishpa were over the temple servants.<sup>22</sup>The overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, of the sons of Asaph, the singers, over the work of the house of God.<sup>23</sup>For there was a command from the king concerning them, and a fixed provision for the singers, as every day required.<sup>24</sup>And Pethahiah the son of Meshezabel, of the sons of Zerah the son of Judah, was at the king's side in all matters concerning the people.<sup>25</sup>And as for the villages, with their fields, some of the people of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba and its villages, and in Dibon and its villages, and in Jekabzeel and its villages,<sup>26</sup>and in Jeshua and in Moladah and Beth-pelet,<sup>27</sup>in Hazar-shual, in Beersheba and its villages,<sup>28</sup>in Ziklag, in Meconah and its villages,<sup>29</sup>in En-rimmon, in Zorah, in Jarmuth,<sup>30</sup>Zanoah, Adullam, and their villages, Lachish and its fields, and Azekah and its villages. So they encamped from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom.<sup>31</sup>The people of Benjamin also lived from Geba onward, at Michmash, Aija, Bethel and its villages,<sup>32</sup>Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah,<sup>33</sup>Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim,<sup>34</sup>Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat,<sup>35</sup>Lod, and Ono, the valley of craftsmen.<sup>36</sup>And certain divisions of the Levites in Judah were assigned to Benjamin.
11.overview: The empty city of 7:4 is filled. The leaders live in Jerusalem, one family in ten is chosen by lot to move there, and the people bless those who volunteer (vv. 1-2). The residents are listed: valiant men of Judah and Benjamin (vv. 3-9), priests under Seraiah (vv. 10-14), Levites with a descendant of Asaph the leader of the praise (vv. 15-18), gatekeepers, temple servants and singers (vv. 19-24). Then the villages of Judah and Benjamin, from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom and on to Lod and Ono (vv. 25-36).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The leaders live in Jerusalem, and the rest cast lots so that one family in ten moves to the holy city while nine in ten remain in their towns (v. 1). The people bless those who willingly offer to live there (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: The empty city of 7:4 is filled by a tithe of the people: one family in ten, chosen by lot, and others who volunteered. They gave God a tenth of their harvest in chapter 10; here they give him a tenth of themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the leaders of the people lived in Jerusalem. And the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in Jerusalem the holy city, while nine out of ten remained in the other towns. And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The problem was stated in 7:4: the city was large and its people few. A wall round an empty city defends nothing. So the leaders move in, the rest cast lots, and one family in every ten packs up and moves to Jerusalem.

It was not an easy lot to draw. Jerusalem was the most exposed place in the province, hated by its neighbours, short of houses, and far from the fields that fed a family. To move meant leaving land your family worked for a half-built city on a hill.

Should Christians cast lots to find God's will? In Israel the lot was a recognised way of leaving a fair choice to God (Prov 16:33), and the apostles used it once, before Pentecost, to fill Judas's place (Acts 1:26). After the Spirit was given, the church is never again seen casting lots; it decides by Scripture, prayer and counsel (Acts 15:28). A lot may still settle a fair choice between equal options, but it is not a way of hearing God speak.

Jerusalem the holy city. Isaiah had called her that (Isa 52:1), and the name followed her into the Gospels (Matt 4:5). But its last use is the one this chapter is reaching for: I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God (Rev 21:2). There, nobody has to be chosen by lot to live in it.

Some did not wait for the lot. They volunteered, and the people blessed them for it. It is what the psalm says of the Messiah's people: Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power (Ps 110:3). The willingness is itself his gift, worked by his power, and it is still the mark of Christ's people: not conscripts but volunteers. In the place he has put you, is there a harder post that needs someone to offer, and have you been waiting to be chosen for it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–24 — The Chiefs Who Lived in Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heads living in Jerusalem: men of Judah and Benjamin (vv. 3-9), priests under Seraiah (vv. 10-14), Levites under Mattaniah, the leader of the praise (vv. 15-18), gatekeepers (v. 19), and temple servants, singers, and Pethahiah at the king's side (vv. 20-24).
verseByVerse.theology: A city of soldiers, priests, singers and gatekeepers: valiant men and the leader of the praise on the same list. The holy city needed both.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the chiefs of the province who lived in Jerusalem; but in the towns of Judah everyone lived on his property in their towns: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the descendants of Solomon's servants. And in Jerusalem lived certain of the sons of Judah and of the sons of Benjamin. Of the sons of Judah: Athaiah the son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, of the sons of Perez; and Maaseiah the son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite. All the sons of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were 468 valiant men. And these are the sons of Benjamin: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah, and his brothers, men of valor, 928. Joel the son of Zichri was their overseer; and Judah the son of Hassenuah was second over the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chiefs are listed family by family, their ancestry traced back several generations. First Judah: 468 valiant men of the sons of Perez (v. 6).

Perez was one of the twin sons of Judah by Tamar, and from Perez came Boaz, David and the kings (Ruth 4:18-22). And in verse 24 the other twin appears: Pethahiah, of the sons of Zerah. Matthew names them both at the start of the genealogy of Jesus: Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar (Matt 1:3). Both branches of that unlikely family were living in Jerusalem.

Then Benjamin, 928, with Judah son of Hassenuah second over the city: together 1,396 fighting men. The holy city still needed soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin, Seraiah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, ruler of the house of God, and their brothers who did the work of the house, 822; and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and his brothers, heads of fathers' houses, 242; and Amashsai, the son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer, and their brothers, mighty men of valor, 128; their overseer was Zabdiel the son of Haggedolim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests, in three groups, 1,192 in all, under Seraiah ... ruler of the house of God (v. 11). His line runs back through Hilkiah, probably the high priest who found the book of the law in Josiah's day (the list skips generations), to Zadok, Solomon's high priest. The house of Zadok had come through the exile unbroken.

Some of the priests are mighty men of valor. In a city under threat, holiness and bravery were not two different kinds of people.

verseByVerse.quote: And of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni; and Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chiefs of the Levites, who were over the outside work of the house of God; and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, who was the leader of the praise, who gave thanks, and Bakbukiah, the second among his brothers; and Abda the son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun. All the Levites in the holy city were 284. The gatekeepers, Akkub, Talmon and their brothers, who kept watch at the gates, were 172.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites include men over the outside work of the house of God, the repairs and supplies, and Mattaniah, of the sons of Asaph, the leader of the praise. Asaph was David's chief musician, and twelve psalms bear his name (Pss 50, 73-83). Five centuries on, his descendant is leading the thanksgiving in the rebuilt temple.

Then the gatekeepers: the gates Nehemiah had hung (7:1) now had men to keep them. Praise inside and watchmen at the doors: that is still what a church needs.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of Israel, and of the priests and the Levites, were in all the towns of Judah, every one in his inheritance. But the temple servants lived on Ophel; and Ziha and Gishpa were over the temple servants. The overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, of the sons of Asaph, the singers, over the work of the house of God. For there was a command from the king concerning them, and a fixed provision for the singers, as every day required. And Pethahiah the son of Meshezabel, of the sons of Zerah the son of Judah, was at the king's side in all matters concerning the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His inheritance: the family land allotted in Joshua's day, returned to after the exile. The nine in ten who stayed were not failing to answer a call. They were living on the land God had promised them.

The temple servants lived on Ophel, where they had built their stretch of wall (3:26). The king who provided for the singers is probably the Persian king, who had already exempted them from tax (Ezra 7:24). If so, an emperor who worshipped other gods was paying the daily wages of the choir that sang Asaph's psalms to the LORD.
